Katherine watches from the bay window as the men argue around her husband's chair. The Mob remains a forceful drama about principle in politics, written when Galsworthy was at his most engaged.
29147-educational-work-of-the-boy-scouts:
Lorne W. Barclay, director of the Department of Education of the Boy Scouts of America, wrote this bulletin for the United States Bureau of Education in 1921. Issued as Bulletin 1921, number 41, and drawn from the Biennial Survey of Education, it cost five cents from the Superintendent of Documents. Barclay examines what scouting added to American education.

Chapters cover scouting and the schools, scouting and citizenship, the pioneer scout, scouting and Americanization, and sea scouting as a branch of the movement. Barclay also reports the National Council's effort to learn vital facts about the boyhood of the nation. Readers get an official early account of scouting as an educational force, in the movement's own confident terms.
29153-poppy-s-presents:
Mrs. Walton, author of Christie's Old Organ, wrote this children's book for the Religious Tract Society in London. Poppy's story runs through thirteen chapters, from The Little Red Cloak and Poppy's Work through a holiday, a long night, and being found at last. Later chapters bring a visit from grandmother, Jacky and Jemmy, and a mother's legacy.

The tale opens as a great cathedral bell strikes twelve, the bell by which the whole city sets its clocks. School children love it best, for its stroke means freedom. Poppy's presents, a ring, a wonderful fire, and at last her father's homecoming, shape a moral story for young readers. Readers get a gentle Victorian children's tale, warm and earnest, about a girl, her gifts, and her family.
29260-sure-pop-and-the-safety-scouts:
Roy Rutherford Bailey published this boys' book in 1916 with the World Book Company, under the auspices of the National Safety Council, copyrighted in 1915. Colonel Sure Pop's motto frames the book: being a Safety Scout means doing the right thing at the right time. The Safety Scout's platform is safety first, the prevention of accidents.

Adventures follow Bob thirsting for adventure and getting it. There is a royal signet ring, a woman and a wizard, and a persistent pigmy. A magic button gives warning, a live wire threatens, and Betty evens the score. Each adventure teaches a safety lesson through story. Readers get a period safety book for children, where thrills carry instruction and every escapade ends with a habit worth keeping.
29271-the-issahar-artifacts:
J. F. Bone wrote this science fiction story framed as a discovered manuscript. The manuscript, the tale says, was found while digging a side passage linking streamways in Narhil Province near Issahar on Kwashior. An excavator passing through a small valley was jammed by oxidized metallic fragments, though Kwashior shows no recorded history of metal artifacts.

A terrestrial operator reported the stoppage, and Assasul, the district engineering monitor, ordered a careful dig in case the artifacts held cultural significance. The debris proved to be remnants of an ancient spaceship. Bone opens with a Lincoln saying, applied across eons: a speck of one-celled plant life parsecs away proves it for the galaxy. Readers get a clever frame tale about archaeology, evidence, and first contact.
29373-educational-work-of-the-girl-scout:
Louise Stevens Bryant was educational secretary of the Girl Scouts. She wrote this bulletin for the United States Bureau of Education in 1921. It is number 46, drawn from the Biennial Survey of Education, 1918 to 1920. It cost five cents from the Superintendent of Documents. Bryant examines Girl Scouting as education, not only as recreation.

Contents cover history and growth, activities, methods, and organization. Bryant opens by asking whether girls should like home work, cooking, cleaning, and minding the baby, and whether a girl should care for her clothes and be able to mend. Readers get an official early account of the Girl Scouts as a training system, in the movement's own practical terms, companion to the Boy Scouts bulletin of the same year.
29440-leading-articles-on-various-subjec:
Hugh Miller, author of The Old Red Sandstone, wrote these leading articles, edited by his son-in-law, the Reverend John Davidson, in a fourth edition published in Edinburgh in 1872 by William P. Nimmo. Miller, the Scottish stonemason turned geologist and editor, wrote leaders for his newspaper on the questions of his day. Davidson selected them to preserve Miller's mature opinion.

Contents include thoughts on the educational question, Lord Brougham, the Scott Monument, and the late Mr. Kemp. Annie McDonald and the Fifeshire forester, a Highland clearing, the poet Montgomery, criticism and internal evidence, and the sanctities of matter follow. Readers get a Victorian editor's mind at work, strong on education, church, and Scotland, in articles meant for the morning paper.
29500-mummery-a-tale-of-three-idealists:
Gilbert Cannan's 1918 novel, published in London by W. Collins Sons, follows three idealists who descend on London and try to live by dreams in a city of fact. Chapters move from dwellers in enchantment and imperium to behind the scenes, the other woman, birds and fishes, supper, solitude, and magic. Then the tale goes out to the English lakes and back to Charing Cross Road. Cannan, author of Mendel and The Stucco House, writes with wit and a satirist's eye.

The three dreamers chase art, love, and freedom, and find each prize costs more than they planned. Mummery, or play-acting, becomes both their refuge and their trap. Readers who enjoy novels of artistic London between the wars will find a clever, bittersweet study of ideals tested by daily life.
29611-william-shakespeare-his-homes-and-:
S. L. Bensusan, general editor of the Pilgrim Books, wrote William Shakespeare: His Homes and Haunts, printed in London and Edinburgh by T. C. and E. C. Jack, with twelve crayon drawings by A. Forrestier and four portraits. Its chapters run from Stratford-on-Avon and the poet's youth through nature round Stratford and Shottery, to first days in London, Shakespeare's London, and the stage in his day.

Bensusan argues that to read a great master, or study a great painter, without first-hand knowledge of the country each lived in, misses half the work. The book walks the reader through Shakespeare's places. Lovers of Shakespeare and of literary travel will find a charming, illustrated pilgrimage.
29682-erdgeist-earth-spirit-a-tragedy-in:
Frank Wedekind's Erdgeist, or Earth-Spirit, a tragedy in four acts translated by Samuel A. Eliot, Jr., was printed in New York in 1914 by Albert and Charles Boni. Its stage directions open on an animal tamer with long black curls, white cravat, vermilion dress coat, white trousers, and white top boots, carrying a whip in his left hand. Wedekind's heroine Lulu steps from that world of show and desire.

Wedekind's verse declares that nature made him from ranker stuff, and lust draws him to the earth. The tragedy follows Lulu through men who want her and a society that judges her. Readers of modern drama will find a landmark of expressionist theatre, bold, erotic, and unsettling.
29713-the-balladists:
John Geddie wrote this short study of ballads for the Famous Scots Series, printed in Edinburgh and London. He starts with a warning: the ballad world has almost no dates, names, or solid landmarks to guide a reader. In Geddie's account, no single maker stands out from the singing crowd, because the balladist counts only as one voice among many, with a life that rarely comes into view.

Seven chapters follow ballad traits, growth, history, structure, and style. Then Geddie treats the mythological ballad, the romantic ballad, and the historical ballad in turn. Old lays of war, woe, joy, treachery, and faery fill his examples. The book is a clear first guide to a form made by many hands and owned by none.
29789-poppa-needs-shorts:
Walt and Leigh Richmond wrote this humorous science fiction tale, with pictures by John Schoenherr. Its headnote warns that valid data can lead to wrong conclusions, while a wrong conclusion can still yield a right answer. Little Oley, aged four, has wandered again into forbidden ground: the ham shack of his big brother Sven, aged fourteen. Glowing bottles lure him, and he pretends to know all their mysteries.

Sven, one of the best ham operators extant, holds contacts with eighteen countries and thirty-eight states. He probes an open chassis with a hot soldering iron, hunting a short. Oley asks what makes shorts, and Sven must explain, from his superior eminence, that a short is when electricity finds a way back without doing its work. The tale turns a pun into a lesson.
29850-woodrow-wilson-s-administration-an:
Frank B. Lord and James William Bryan compiled this record of Woodrow Wilson's administration and achievements, printed in Washington in 1921. The subtitle calls it a compilation from the newspaper press of eight years of the world's greatest history, particularly as concerns America, its people, and their affairs. A portrait in typophotogravure shows Wilson at America's entry into the war, from a charcoal sketch by Hattie E. Burdette.

The book opens with Americanism, from Wilson's Independence Hall address of July 14, 1914. Patriotism, Wilson says there, lies in practical, everyday duty: to love America is to love the duty nearest one's hand. History's Proving Ground follows, with the eight years of administration set out from press reports. The volume is a period scrapbook of a presidency, made while its events were still fresh.
29888-the-hunting-of-the-snark-an-agony-:
Lewis Carroll, author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, published The Hunting of the Snark in London in 1876, with Macmillan and Company. Henry Holiday drew nine pictures for the book. Carroll calls it an Easter greeting to every child who loves Alice, and inscribes it to a dear child, in memory of golden summer hours and whispers of a summer sea.

The subtitle calls the poem an agony in eight fits, and the fits carry the hunt forward in nonsense verse. A boyish garb, a spade, and a friendly knee open the dedicatory verses, where a girl asks questions as she rests. The poem that follows is Carroll's most famous nonsense quest, told with wordplay, logic turned sideways, and pictures to match. It remains a classic of comic verse for children and grown readers alike.
29976-weak-on-square-roots:
Russell Burton wrote Weak on Square Roots, with pictures by Tom Beecham. Its headnote asks whether a wife calling her husband Pumpkinhead is an insult or a pet name, and whose pet name at that. Ronald Lovegear, fourteen years with Allied Electronix, rides a coach through dusk-darkened Jersey meadows, hugging his burden and cursing the engineer rocking the train. He holds a conviction that the throttle of the 5:10 bound for Philadelphia will someday be worked by an intelligent robot.

Lovegear has talked his superiors into lending him the company's most advanced mechanism yet for home work, by a little white lie that morning. Pascal, he told them, is a little weak on square roots, and that did it. Old Hardwick would never let an Allied computer reach the market unless it mastered square roots absolutely.
30139-the-beauties-of-the-state-of-washi:
Harry F. Giles, deputy commissioner of the State Bureau of Statistics and Immigration, writes a tourist book on Washington, published at Olympia in 1915. The rhododendron, the state flower, fronts the volume in a photograph by Asahel Curtis, and chapters cover the Evergreen State, its mountains, forests, and climate. Puget Sound follows, with yachting, Hood Canal, commerce, east shores, and island groups such as San Juan and Whidby.

Later sections cross the Olympic Peninsula and the harbor country of Grays Harbor and Willapa Bay, then Mount Rainier National Park and the Columbia River. The Inland Empire closes the tour, with the Yakima, Wenatchee, and Chelan valleys, the Okanogan highlands, Spokane, the wheat plateau, and Walla Walla. The book sells a young state to travelers, in pictures and plain praise.
30170-lonesome-hearts:
Russ Winterbotham tells a comic science fiction romance from the view of Yljm, a creature from another planet who falls in love with Mjly. Mjly has no shape and no intelligence, yet Yljm calls her the greatest bit of protoplasm in any galaxy, a lovely soul who talks sweetly in a voice like distant thunder. His own green body, genes, and chromosomes mark him handsome by his world's standards, and he lies in the sun thinking of love.

Kelly Freas drew the pictures, and the tale turns when Mjly warns that life on their world will end, though the world itself will stand. Yljm, who claims he cannot be subtle and lies badly, must face a doom he first shrugs off as trivial talk. The humor lies in that mismatch: grand cosmic love, told by a narrator who is earnest, vain, and wholly alien.
30201-in-praise-of-folly-illustrated-wit:
Erasmus speaks through Folly herself in a satire illustrated with many curious cuts designed, drawn, and etched by Hans Holbein. Reeves and Turner published the London volume in 1876, with a portrait, a life of Erasmus, and his epistle addressed to Sir Thomas More. Folly's praise turns learning, power, and piety upside down, in the humanist manner that made the work famous across Europe.

The life prefixed to the text follows the Rotterdam statue inscription as most authentic. It gives Erasmus's birth on October 28, 1467, against other lives that give 1465 or a vague year near 1467. His mother, daughter of a physician at Sevenbergen in Holland, opens a life of vast learning, candour, and moderation. Holbein's cuts give the satire a visual wit to match its verbal edge.
30323-the-book-of-religions-comprising-t:
John Hayward, author of the New England Gazetteer, compiles the views, creeds, sentiments, and opinions of all principal religious sects in the world, with church and missionary statistics and biographical sketches. Albert Colby and Company published the Boston volume in 1860, giving special weight to Christian denominations in Europe and America. Lutherans, Calvinists, Hopkinsians, Arians, Socinians, and Humanitarians open the survey, with church government and Presbyterians following.

Later sections treat Cumberland Presbyterians, Episcopalians, the church in the United States, Cambridge and Saybrook platforms, Moravians, Tunkers, and Mennonites. Disciples of Christ, Friends or Quakers, Shakers, Reformed churches Dutch and German, Restorationists, Universalists, Roman Catholics, and Methodists Episcopal and Protestant all find places. Hayward offers a mid-century reference shelf in one volume, for readers who want sects compared side by side. The aim is plain: each group is set out in short terms, so a reader can see what it holds.
30433-e-mile-or-concerning-education-ext:
Jean Jacques Rousseau's Emile, or Concerning Education, appears here in extracts chosen by Jules Steeg, with an introduction and notes, translated by Eleanor Worthington and entered for copyright in 1888. Steeg keeps the core teaching ideas found in Rousseau's opening three books.

The translator notes that Steeg helps French and American teachers by choosing well. The full three-volume novel, with long disquisitions and digressions dear to patient ancestors, now feels distasteful to all but lovers of curious books. These extracts give teachers Rousseau's core ideas on nature, learning, and childhood in a usable form.
30451-a-day-with-keats:
May Byron imagines a day with John Keats in this volume from the Days with the Great Poets series, uniform with companion books on Browning, Burns, Longfellow, Shakespeare, and Tennyson. The scene opens about eight on an early summer morning, with a young man strolling in the garden at Wentworth Place, Hampstead.

Keats lives in one of only two houses there, sharing rooms with his friend Charles Armitage Brown, while Mrs. Brawne and her family occupy the other. Byron uses the garden, the wooden houses, and their leafy draperies to stage a close, readable portrait of the poet at home. The book offers biography as a visit, letting a reader spend a morning in Keats's world.
30498-two-maiden-aunts:
Mary H. Debenham writes Two Maiden Aunts, published in London in 1895 by the National Society's Repository and in New York by Thomas Whittaker, with two full-page illustrations by Gertrude D. Hammond. Debenham, author of Mistress Phil, A Little Candle, and Fairmeadows Farm, opens with chapters titled The Aunts and The Nephew.

Later chapters add the first day, a heart of oak, the wrong end, Christmas at Oakfield, hero and heroines, and travel in the Channel and in port. A frontispiece shows the two maiden aunts themselves. Debenham writes a gentle domestic tale of aunts, a nephew, home life, and small moral lessons, in the Victorian girls' book tradition.
30562-unfinished-portraits-stories-of-mu:
Jennette Lee writes Unfinished Portraits, stories of musicians and artists, published in New York in September 1916 by Charles Scribner's Sons. Lee, author of Kate Wetherill, A Pillar of Salt, The Son of a Fiddler, and Uncle William, dedicates the book to Gerald Stanley Lee. The dedication adds the great road from the seen to the unseen.

Contents open with There Was in Florence a Lady, Thumbs and Fugues, and A Window of Music, then turn to Frederic Chopin and other masters. Subjects named on the title page include Schubert, Titian, Chopin, Giorgione, Bach, Leonardo, and Albrecht Durer. Lee sketches artists as people, not just names, in stories that feel like portraits left deliberately open.
30657-sovereign-grace-its-source-its-nat:
D. L. Moody writes Sovereign Grace, its source, its nature, and its effects, with three gospel dialogues, copyrighted in 1891 by Fleming H. Revell of Chicago, New York, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh. Its epigraph quotes Ephesians: by grace are ye saved.

A prefatory note says the faithful ambassador of Christ must proclaim God's full counsel, dividing truth rightly, to all hearers. He must warn the openly wicked that just judgments will overtake persistence in evil, unmask the hypocrite, and protest the crooked ways of self-seekers and time-servers. Yet no work delights him more, Moody adds, than entering his master's spirit in preaching grace.
30690-the-casual-ward-academic-and-other:
A. D. Godley writes The Casual Ward, Academic and Other Oddments, published in London in 1912 by Smith, Elder. Contents open with a Latin oration on the Bodleian law, The Eights in Fiction in old and new or Kodak style, Thucydides on influenza, and Herodotus on horseback.

Later pieces add Tacitus history book six, The Journalistic Touch, The True Tale of Troy, Forgotten History, and essays on bribery and the people's will. The Tutor's Expedient, The Tortured Tutor, The Difficulties of Mr. Bull, and The Nation in Arms follow. Godley blends classical parody, Oxford humor, and topical wit into a clever miscellany for learned readers.
30810-the-wolf-patrol-a-tale-of-baden-po:
John Finnemore wrote this tale of Baden-Powell's Boy Scouts, first published in October 1908 and held here in an edition of 1922, reprinted in 1923. Finnemore, author of Jack Haydon's Quest and Two Boys in War-time, dedicates the book by special permission to Lieutenant-General R. S. S. Baden-Powell, founder of the movement on which the story is based. Its frontispiece shows a figure called Chippy.

The book opens with the Scout Law, in nine points. A scout's honour is to be trusted, a scout is loyal, useful, and a friend to all, courteous, a friend to animals, obedient, cheerful, and thrifty. The Wolf Patrol story then puts those rules to work in camp and country adventure. Young readers get a wholesome early scout tale, full of outdoor skill and the spirit of the new movement.
30834-fairy-tales-from-the-german-forest:
Frau Arndt wrote this book of fairy tales from the German forests, published in London by Everett and Company. It is dedicated to her daughters Margaret and Barbara and her nephews Charles and Stephen Johnson. An introductory poem says she first learned fairy stories in English lanes, among honeysuckle and wild roses, and in London parks. Since she came to Germany, the poem says, the good folk speak to her more often in their native home.

The first tale, What's the Use of It, opens in a village near the great forest, where a little girl named Hansi Herzchen lives as the seventh child of seven. Arndt's tales mix forest wonder with home feeling, in the old fairy style. Young readers, and adults reading aloud, will find gentle magic, woodland creatures, and morals tucked inside the fun.
30909-the-church-her-books-and-her-sacra:
E. E. Holmes, bachelor of divinity and Archdeacon of London, wrote this course of instructions given at All Saints, Margaret Street, in Lent 1910. It is held here in a new impression from Longmans, Green in 1914. Holmes had also written In Watchings Often, for nurses and others, and Prayer and Action, on prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. This book speaks to churchgoers who want to grasp what their church is and what it does.

Contents open with an introduction and a chapter on the church itself, then turn to the church's books: first the Bible, then the Prayer Book. A closing part treats the church's sacraments, the rites by which faith is lived and sealed. Holmes writes in clear, pastoral prose, with the Anglican tradition at its center. It is a useful guide for readers who want a short, orderly account of church, scripture, worship, and sacraments.
30942-extensions-of-known-ranges-of-mexi:
Sydney Anderson wrote this short paper on extensions of known ranges of Mexican bats. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 9, number 9, pages 347 to 351, on August 15, 1956. The bats were taken incidentally to studies of speciation in North American mammals, made possible by help from the National Science Foundation and the Kansas University Endowment Association.

Several bats turned up outside the geographic limits previously recorded for them. Pending more detailed faunal accounts, Anderson publishes these notes so the distributional records will be available to students of Mexican mammals. Most of these bats live chiefly in the tropics, so the fresh records push their ranges farther north along Mexico's east coast or along its west coast. It is a compact, useful paper for mammal researchers.
31029-i-ll-leave-it-to-you-a-light-comed:
Noel Coward's light comedy in three acts, published by Samuel French with copyright dated 1920, is one of the playwright's early stage works, issued in the firm's standard acting edition. The volume carries the usual French apparatus of the day: a full copyright warning, royalty terms, and rules for amateur performance. They include the need for a paid licence before any public staging.

As a printed play text, it lets readers and amateur companies study Coward's early comic voice at close range, before his later fame. The comedy form itself, three brisk acts built on talk, timing, and social sparring, shows the young dramatist already working in the witty, well-bred register that would soon make his name.
31034-by-ways-in-book-land-short-essays-:
William Davenport Adams, author of the Dictionary of English Literature, wrote this book of short essays on literary subjects. It was published by Elliot Stock in London in 1888 and affectionately inscribed to his father, W. H. Davenport Adams. Its epigraph, from Georgics book 4, reads Excursusque breves tentat, short excursions are attempted. Adams calls his book By-Ways in Book-Land for a reason.

In his preface he says he deals with small subjects in an unelaborate manner. He leaves the highways of literature to stray into fields and lanes, picking here a flower and there a leaf, and never going far. His essays include Paper-Knife Pleasures, Ruskin as Poet, Elections in Literature, Familiar Verse, Shakespeare's England, Heredity in Song, Stings for the Stingy, Dialogues of the Dead, and Sermons in Flowers. They end with Don Quixote in England. It is a modest, charming ramble through books.
31097-froebel-s-gifts:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith's 1895 volume, published by Houghton, Mifflin, explains Friedrich Froebel's gifts for kindergarten teaching. Taking Froebel's image of the kindergarten as a free republic of childhood, the authors devote a chapter to each gift in turn. The gifts run from the first soft ball through the building gifts, blocks, tablets, sticks, and rings. They close with general remarks on their use.

Each gift is meant to teach through handling: shape, color, number, and form learned by play before words. Written for teachers and parents, the book remains a clear guide to Froebel's system, showing how simple objects were meant to train perception, thought, and the hand together.
31112-the-scarlet-stigma-a-drama-in-four:
James Edgar Smith's 1899 drama, printed in Washington, adapts Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter for the stage in four acts. Its persons include Roger Prynne, called Chillingworth, the youthful divine Arthur Dimsdell, Governor Bellingham, Hester Prynne, and Satan himself, who appears as a hallucination of Dimsdell's troubled mind.

Smith's prefatory note explains that the third scene of the second act is a transcript from Dimsdell's diseased consciousness. It adds that the stigma on his breast marks the climax of an auto-hypnotic trance. Set in Boston in June 1668, the play turns Hawthorne's novel of guilt and secrecy into stage action, with a psychological reading of its most famous scenes.
31121-a-calendar-of-scottish-saints:
Dom Michael Barrett's Calendar of Scottish Saints, printed at the Fort Augustus Abbey Press in a revised second edition in 1919, gives a saint for each day of the year. January opens with St. Ernan, disciple and reputed nephew of St. Columba, who died as abbot of Drumhome in 640 and gave his name to Killernan in Ross-shire, followed by St. Chroman of Ayrshire and the recluse St. Kentigerna.

Barrett notes frankly where Reformation destruction of records leaves a life nearly blank, and where a church dedication is all that survives. Devotional and scholarly at once, the calendar preserves the scattered memory of Scotland's early holy men and women.
31325-an-annotated-checklist-of-nebraska:
Olin L. Webb and J. Knox Jones Jr.'s 1952 checklist, volume 5, number 21 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, annotates the bats of Nebraska. Its history begins with Harrison Allen's 1864 monograph, the first mention of Nebraska bats, listing forms collected in Nebraska Territory by J. G. Cooper on his 1857 journey. Allen gave no exact localities or dates, and Cooper's specimens no longer exist in the United States National Museum, save one traded to the British Museum in 1866. The authors therefore exclude those records from the state's list.

Myron H. Swenk's 1908 account, listing six kinds, provides the next baseline, and the checklist builds from there into the modern annotated fauna of Nebraska's bats.
31374-the-dramatist-or-stop-him-who-can-:
Frederick Reynolds's The Dramatist, or Stop Him Who Can, is a comedy in five acts. It was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, and printed from the prompt book under the authority of the managers, with remarks by Mrs. Inchbald. Its hero is Vapid, a would-be playwright who cries, in the illustration caption, that he will write both prologue and epilogue. The comedy turns on a man who cannot stop writing plays, and on the people who must endure him.

Reynolds, a prolific dramatist of his day, satirizes the theater world from inside: authors, managers, and audiences all get their turn. The play's humor comes from Vapid's tireless, misplaced confidence. Readers of Georgian comedy will find a lively, theatrical farce, preserved here in the acting version used on the Covent Garden stage.
31397-the-earl-of-essex-a-tragedy-in-fiv:
Henry Jones's The Earl of Essex is a tragedy in five acts. It was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, and printed from the prompt book under the authority of the managers, with remarks by Mrs. Inchbald. An illustration shows the Earl of Essex in act four, scene one, speaking the line about a ring as a private mark of faith between himself and the queen. The play dramatizes the fall of Elizabeth's favorite, caught between ambition, love, and royal suspicion.

Jones writes in the formal tragic manner of the Georgian stage, where high rank and high passion meet a fatal end. The remarks and the prompt-book text preserve the play as audiences actually saw it. Readers of eighteenth-century drama will find a serviceable, affecting tragedy of court intrigue, with Essex's ring as its most memorable device.
31451-a-little-question-in-ladies-rights:
Parker H. Fillmore's A Little Question in Ladies' Rights is a humorous story of a girl named Margery Blair and her young neighbor Willie Jones. Part one opens with Margery sitting under a cherry tree, waiting with a certain air of expectancy. Willie pops over the back fence with a tin pail, but Margery gazes tensely into nothing: Willie, evidently, is not the object of her thoughts. She explains, frankly, that she ate a whole bagful of bananas and is waiting to be sick, as Effie predicted.

The comedy that follows, including a mud plaster mixed by united efforts and Margery's unwomanly persistence, as the narrator puts it, turns on a small girl's claim to her own way. The ladies' rights of the title are played for laughs, yet the story treats Margery's determination seriously. Readers will find a light, period piece about childhood, appetite, and stubbornness.
31463-the-orphan-or-the-unhappy-marriage:
Thomas Otway's The Orphan, or The Unhappy Marriage, is a tragedy in five acts, correctly given as performed at the Theatres Royal, with remarks. The remarks note that after its 1680 debut at the Duke's Theatre, the play enjoyed a long run on the stage. Its revival owed much, the remarks say, to the great merit of Miss O'Neil in the role of Monimia. The language of the play is poetical and tender, and its incidents affecting.

The plot turns on a marriage gone wrong, with love, betrayal, and fatal misunderstanding driving the action to tragedy. Otway, a leading Restoration dramatist, writes for actors and audiences who prized passion expressed in verse. Readers of Restoration drama will find one of his most durable works, still affecting in its study of trust broken and love misdirected.
31503-contemporary-russian-novelists:
Frederick Eisemann translated Serge Persky's survey of recent Russian fiction from the French, and John W. Luce and Company published it in Boston in 1913. Its nine chapters open with a brief survey of Russian literature, then take up one novelist at a time. The chapters cover Anton Tchekoff, Vladimir Korolenko, and Vikenty Veressayev in the spellings the book prints.

They continue with Maxim Gorky, Leonid Andreyev, and Dmitry Merezhkovsky, then Alexander Kuprin, and close with writers in vogue. Persky's book gives English readers a guided tour of the leading Russian novelists of his day, with each figure treated in a chapter of his own.
3151-the-city-of-domes-a-walk-with-an-ar:
John D Barry walks the Panama-Pacific International Exposition with an architect in this guide. The courts and palaces of San Francisco's 1915 fair give the book its ground. Domes, towers, and colored walls rise in the text as they rose on the fairgrounds, and the architect explains what each building was meant to do.

Barry writes for the visitor who wants more than a glance. He pairs description with judgment, noting where the fair's beauty serves its purpose and where it merely dazzles. The book now doubles as a record: the fair is gone, but its courts survive here in words, for readers who want to see a vanished city of domes.
31525-james-gilmour-of-mongolia-his-diar:
James Gilmour of Mongolia, his diaries, letters, and reports, was edited and arranged by Richard Lovett. It was published in London by the Religious Tract Society in 1895, in a third and cheaper edition, with a portrait, two maps, and five illustrations. Gilmour, a missionary in Mongolia, left diaries and letters that Lovett, author of Norwegian Pictures, shaped into a life. An opening hymn quoted in the book speaks of peace and joy found in Christ alone, after long sighing for rest and happiness.

The volume follows Gilmour's work among Mongolian peoples: travel, preaching, hardship, and friendship. Its diaries give the day-to-day texture of missionary life on the steppe. Readers of missionary biography and of Mongolian history will find a vivid, firsthand record, edited with care for a popular audience.
31543-a-concise-anglo-saxon-dictionary-f:
John R. Clark Hall's A Concise Anglo-Saxon Dictionary for the Use of Students, in a second edition revised and enlarged, was published by the Macmillan Company of New York in 1916. It was printed at Cambridge by the University Press. The dictionary gives Old English words with their meanings, grammar, and forms, for students reading Anglo-Saxon texts. Its transcriber's note explains the spelling and alphabetizing rules: the letter æ counts as ae, eth is alphabetized separately after t, with j and v absent from the alphabet.

Entries are concise, with cross-references, variant spellings, and inflected forms noted. Short entries, mostly cross-references, ran two or three to a line in print, and are separated in this e-text. For students of Old English, Clark Hall's dictionary remains a standard desk reference, compact enough to use beside a text.
31567-the-lawyers-a-drama-in-five-acts:
The Lawyers, a drama in five acts, translated from the German of Augustus William Iffland by C. Ludger, was printed in London by J. W. Myers for W. West in 1799, at two shillings and sixpence. Iffland, a leading German dramatist and actor, wrote for a stage where law, family, and reputation collided, and Ludger's translation brought his play to English readers. An advertisement fronts the volume, as was customary for plays of the period.

The drama turns on lawyers and their clients, with the profession itself on trial in comic and serious scenes. Iffland's work, popular across Europe, offered English audiences a German view of legal life. Readers of eighteenth-century drama in translation will find a serviceable, interesting example of the continental repertoire as London knew it.
31592-cato-a-tragedy-in-five-acts:
Joseph Addison's Cato, a tragedy in five acts, was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, and printed from the prompt book under the authority of the managers, with remarks by Mrs. Inchbald. This edition was printed at Paris for Baudry in 1823. The remarks tell how Addison was born so frail that he was christened at once, for fear he would soon die. The English owe their choicest moral works to his vigorous mind, the remarks say.

The play itself dramatizes Cato the Younger, the Roman republican who chose death rather than submission to Caesar. Addison's blank verse and moral argument made Cato a favorite of the eighteenth century, quoted by patriots on both sides of the Atlantic. Readers of Augustan drama will find a tragedy of principle, where a single man's stand becomes a lesson in liberty.
31667-the-nephews-a-play-in-five-acts:
William Augustus Iffland's comedy, freely translated from German by Hannibal Evans Lloyd, is a five-act play printed in London in 1799, the year shown on its title page in Roman numerals. Its cast centers on Chancellor Fleffel, his son the Counsellor, the merchant Mr. Drave, and the two Brooks brothers, Lewis and Philip.

The opening act finds the Counsellor and Lewis at breakfast in the Chancellor's house, trading jokes about family stiffness, love, and a grave, melancholy brother to beware of. Readers get a late eighteenth-century stage comedy of households, guardians, and young men maneuvering for favor and marriage.
31671-plain-talks-on-avoided-subjects:
Henry N. Guernsey, a physician and former professor of obstetrics, wrote this plain-spoken guide for parents and young people on subjects most adults of his day shrank from teaching. Drawing on forty years of medical practice, he argues that ignorance, not knowledge, leads young men and women into sexual harm.

The talks cover chastity, the risks of uninstructed youth, and the duty of parents and guardians to speak truthfully and squarely. Readers get a frank nineteenth-century health book, earnest rather than prurient, that treats open instruction as protection for the young.
31682-life-of-john-keats:
William Michael Rossetti's Life of John Keats was published at London by Walter Scott in 1887. Its first chapter follows Keats from his birth in London on October 31, 1795, through school at Enfield under John Clarke, tutored by Charles Cowden Clarke. It continues to the death of his parents and his apprenticeship to the surgeon Hammond. He leaves Hammond, studies surgery, reads Spenser, and takes to poetry.

The chapter then introduces his literary acquaintances, Leigh Hunt, Haydon, J. Hamilton Reynolds, and Dilke, and closes with his first volume, Poems, of 1817. Rossetti's life runs in nine chapters, tracing Keats from a surgeon's apprentice to a poet of lasting fame in a short working life.
31845-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Volume seven of Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, newly translated by Gaston Du C. de Vere and published in London between 1912 and 1914, covers Tribolo to Il Sodoma. The ten-volume edition carries five hundred illustrations.

Its lives include Niccolò called Tribolo, Pierino da Vinci, Baccio Bandinelli, Giuliano Bugiardini, Cristofano Gherardi called Doceno, Jacopo da Pontormo, Simone Mosca, the Genga, and Michele San Michele. They also include Giovanni Antonio Bazzi called Il Sodoma. Readers get Vasari's Renaissance art history in modern English, rich in anecdote about artists, patrons, and works.
31909-doctor-bolus-and-his-patients:
Doctor Bolus and His Patients was published at Troy, New York, by Merriam, Moore and Company. It follows an old-fashioned doctor on his morning rounds, cane in hand, sometimes with his student, a man who took up medicine at thirty in hopes of succeeding Bolus. The book's illustrations include Greediness and Tooth Pulling.

On one morning, Bolus first calls at the Squire's, examines his sick father's tongue, feels his pulse, and mixes a white powder and a gray powder to be taken every two hours. He then visits old black John, a very poor man relieved by a good Quaker, and gives him calomel. Readers get a humorous illustrated tale of country medicine, quaint and kindly.
31938-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Volume eight of Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, newly translated by Gaston Du C. de Vere and published in London between 1912 and 1915, covers Bastiano to Taddeo Zucchero. The ten-volume edition carries five hundred illustrations.

One life follows a young artist placed, through Baldassarre Castiglioni, secretary of the Duke of Mantua and friend of Raffaello, in the school of Raffaello's young men. There he learns to draw and work in color with facility and grace, counterfeiting animals, draperies, instruments, and landscapes. Readers get Vasari's Renaissance lives in modern English, with the workshop gossip and judgments of the master biographer.
32221-the-case-and-exceptions-stories-of:
Frederick Trevor Hill's The Case and Exceptions, stories of counsel and clients, was published in New York by Frederick A. Stokes Company in 1900, second edition, dedicated to M. W. H. Its contents run from Outside the Record and In the Matter of Bateman through The Finding of Fact, A Conclusion of Law, and The Burden of Proof. They continue through In His Own Behalf to The Distant Drum.

The opening story, Outside the Record, begins in General Sessions court, June 5, 1896, as a letter to Dorothy Dear. It is over, the writer says. Warren's fate rests with the jury, and the writer has done the little he could, though strained almost too much. His heart sinks at the thought that he may have left something undone. He may have missed some trap of the district attorney. Readers get legal stories from inside the case.
32362-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Giorgio Vasari's lives of artists appear here in volume nine of a ten-volume translation by Gaston Du C. de Vere, issued in London in 1912 to 1915. This volume opens with Michelagnolo Buonarroti and continues with Francesco Primaticcio, Tiziano da Cadore, Jacopo Sansovino, and Leone Lioni of Arezzo. Later lives cover other Italian craftsmen still living in Vasari's day, and Flemish artists.

Each life pairs career detail with notes on works, patrons, and workshops, so readers see how painters, sculptors, and architects trained, won commissions, and built a name. The volume also carries an index of names and plates in colour, making it a useful entry point to Renaissance art through the artists' own stories.
32392-notes-on-agriculture-in-cyprus-and:
W. Bevan's Notes on Agriculture in Cyprus and Its Products, published in 1919, surveys farming on the island from the post of Director of Agriculture, Cyprus. An opening section covers geography, climate and rainfall, administration, weights, measures, and currency, followed by land tenure, labour, tithes, credit, irrigation, implements, and pests. Livestock chapters treat cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, camels, horses, donkeys, mules, and poultry.

Dairy produce includes milk, cheese, butter, and local products such as xynogala, trachanas, and kaimaki. Crop sections cover cereals such as wheat, barley, and maize, fruits such as vines, citrus, figs, and bananas, nuts, vegetables, and fodders such as carob and lucerne. The book remains a detailed, practical record of Cypriot agriculture in the early twentieth century.
32605-history-of-beasts:
History of Beasts, printed in Portland by Bailey and Noyes, teaches children about familiar animals through short moral sketches. The cat destroys rats and mice and purrs when treated kindly; the dog guards his master's property, barks at strangers, and follows faithfully; the cow gives milk, beef, leather, and horn.

The fox proves cunning and mischievous, troubling farmers by killing geese and chickens, while the goat gives wholesome milk. Each sketch pairs a plain fact about an animal with a lesson for little boys and girls, urging patience, faithfulness, and kindness toward living creatures.
3262-the-pilgrims-of-hope-and-chants-for:
William Morris joins a verse narrative and a set of songs in this 1915 Longmans volume. The Pilgrims of Hope first appeared in The Commonweal between March 1885 and July 1886, its title settled only as publication went on. Chants for Socialists joins it, giving the movement its singing voice. Morris, poet, craftsman, and socialist, wrote both.

The pilgrims travel toward a hope that is political as well as personal: a society remade by labor and fellowship. The chants turn that hope into marching verse, plain and rousing. Readers who know Morris for his crafts and romances will find him here as a prophet: art in service of a cause, and poetry meant to be sung at meetings, not shelved.
32639-the-medici-boots:
Pearl Norton Swet's The Medici Boots, printed in Weird Tales in August and September 1936, opens with boots that lay fifty years under glass in the Dickerson museum. Fashioned of creamy leather and threaded with silver, they are appliqued with sapphire silks and scarlet and tipped with a pale amethyst. They carry a medieval Florentine past.

Old Silas Dickerson brought them from a dusty Florence shop, and died at ninety in his private museum with the boots on his lap. His note to his favorite nephew John Delameter asks that the dangerous possession be destroyed, or else put forever under glass in a public museum.
32687-the-colonists:
Raymond F. Jones tells of a colony on a world where wet and dry years run in a cycle equal to two Earth years. Captain Louis Carnahan counts down the last season in a two-walled hut, drinking from a gourd while biologist Bolinger tends a collection grown over eight years. Most gear has blown away or sunk into the planet.

Later scenes follow Mark Jorden, a farm leader, his daughter Bonnie, and neighbors who test what a colony needs to endure. Doctor Ashby claims any fact can be found with the right test, and a child's death at Maintown puts that claim to proof. The tale asks what qualities let men truly settle a world.
32721-the-history-of-virginia-in-four-pa:
Robert Beverley, a native and inhabitant of Virginia, writes this history in four parts, reprinted from the London edition of 1722 with an introduction by Charles Campbell. The Richmond edition appeared from J. W. Randolph in 1855.

Book one traces the first settlement and government to the year 1706, from Raleigh's letters patent and the Roanoke voyages to Jamestown. Book two treats the natural productions suited to trade. Book three treats the native Indians, their religion, laws, and customs in war and peace. Book four gives the present state of the country as of June 10, 1720.
32883-fresh-light-from-the-ancient-monum:
Archibald Henry Sayce, deputy professor of comparative philology at Oxford, sketches notable ways recent discoveries support the Bible. The discoveries come from Egypt, Palestine, Assyria, Babylonia, and Asia Minor. The book appeared in London from the Religious Tract Society in 1884 in a second edition. A Hittite king's monument from Carchemish, now in the British Museum, fronts the book.

Chapters treat Genesis, the Exodus, and the Moabite Stone with the inscription of Siloam. They treat the empire of the Hittites, the Assyrian invasions, and Nebuchadrezzar and Cyrus. Sayce argues that the forgotten Hittite empire once contended on equal terms with Egypt and Assyria. Inscriptions of Sargon, he writes, prove Isaiah's Assyrian campaign real, not ideal, and the sea of papyrus reeds is not the Red Sea.
33024-moody-s-stories-being-a-second-vol:
D. L. Moody's Stories, a second volume of anecdotes, incidents, and illustrations authorized in 1884, collects the short tales the evangelist used in his preaching. The opening story, Lady Pendulum, tells of a skeptical London lady brought to meetings in her carriage, unable to walk, who feared Moody's words would fade once he returned to America. He answered her with the fable of a clock pendulum that counted its ticks, grew discouraged, and nearly gave up.

The anecdotes that follow work the same way, turning everyday scenes into pictures of faith, perseverance, and hope. Moody's gift was homely illustration, and these stories show it at its most direct. The volume is useful both as a record of revival preaching and as a source of short, plain tales that preachers and teachers have borrowed ever since.
33203-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Giorgio Vasari's lives, in Gaston Du C. De Vere's new translation, reach volume ten in this edition, covering Bronzino to Vasari himself with a general index. Published between 1912 and 1915 in ten volumes with five hundred illustrations, the series gathers the artists of the Italian Renaissance in short, vivid lives. This volume closes the set, joining the academicians of design, painters, sculptors, and architects in one final sweep.

Vasari writes as both artist and storyteller, mixing anecdote, judgment, and workshop detail. De Vere's translation keeps the flavor of the original while making it clear for English readers. For students of art history, the volume is both a reference and a pleasure, capping a classic work that shaped how the Renaissance has been remembered.
33299-the-five-giants:
The Five Giants, revised by D. P. Kidder and published in New York in 1847 for the Sunday-School Union, is a children's tale with a moral heart. It opens with a boy recalling how few things pleased him as a child, then turns to giants who embody faults and follies that young readers must learn to face. The book was made for Sunday schools, where story and lesson went hand in hand.

Its charm lies in its plain, old-fashioned storytelling, where giants are both monsters and metaphors for greed, pride, and sloth. Young readers meet danger and deliverance in short, vivid scenes. For students of children's literature, The Five Giants offers a window on how the 1840s taught virtue through wonder and fear.
33340-weighed-and-wanting-addresses-on-t:
D. L. Moody's Weighed and Wanting, copyrighted in 1898, gives addresses on the Ten Commandments, under the text Tekel: thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. Moody takes each commandment in turn, from the first to the tenth, weighing modern life against God's law. His addresses are plain, earnest, and aimed at ordinary hearers.

The book's power lies in its direct, pastoral style, as Moody presses conscience without academic detour. Each address stands alone, yet the whole builds a searching self-examination. For readers of evangelical classics, Weighed and Wanting remains a clear, challenging guide to the commandments as a mirror for the soul.
33415-pandora-s-box-a-tragedy-in-three-a:
Frank Wedekind's Pandora's Box, a tragedy in three acts translated by Samuel A. Eliot Jr., presents the German playwright's dark, daring drama. Wedekind, whose work shocked his age, writes of a woman whose beauty and fate draw men to ruin, in a play that blends realism with symbol. The translation, published by Boni and Liveright, keeps Wedekind's sharp, unsettling voice.

The play's power lies in its bold portrait of desire, society, and doom, told in scenes of great theatrical force. Its tone is grim yet lyrical, suited to readers of modern drama. For students of Wedekind, Pandora's Box remains a key work, a tragedy that still provokes and disturbs more than a century on.
33456-an-address-to-a-wealthy-libertine-:
An Address to a Wealthy Libertine, or the Melancholy Effects of Seduction, with a letter from an unfortunate farmer's daughter to her parents in Norfolk, is an early nineteenth-century moral tract. It was priced at sixpence. Its opening verse appeals directly to the libertine, recalling a young woman ruined by his arts. The tract was sold by J. Parkerson in Norwich.

The pamphlet's power lies in its plain, urgent moral appeal, using one girl's ruin to warn the rich against seduction. Its tone is earnest and sorrowful, not prurient, and its letter gives the victim a voice. For students of social history, it is a revealing source on how the age preached against a common wrong.
33733-the-guarded-heights:
Wadsworth Camp writes a novel of ambition, love, and social climbing in this 1921 Doubleday book, in five parts: Oakmont, Princeton, the Market-Place, the Forest, and the New World. George Morton cannot say when he first formed the absurd notion that Sylvia Planter should be his. The realization comes all at once, destroying his dreary outlook and urging him to fantastic heights and curious depths.

After a precarious rural education, George tried to rescue his father's livery business from cheap automobiles that persistently undermined it. He knew horses and rode better than any hunting gentleman of the rich countryside. No one near his age could stand up to him in argument, yet he craved broader worlds to conquer. Failure, the vast Planter estate, and Sylvia's arrival change everything. Camp writes a sharp story of class, desire, and American change.
33874-wild-bees-wasps-and-ants-and-other:
Edward Saunders, fellow of the Royal and Linnean Societies, describes wild bees, wasps, and ants, and other stinging insects, in this Routledge volume with four coloured plates by Constance A. Saunders. Contents move from the subject in general through solitary groups, solitary bees, cuckoo bees, fossors or diggers, solitary wasps, and social groups. They continue with ants, social wasps, humble bees, bees with bifid and pointed tongues, leaf-cutting bees, Osmia and its habits, a colony of Anthophora, bees and pollen-collecting, and bees' tongues and honey-sucking.

Plates show Formica sanguinea in male, female, and worker forms, Mutilla europaea, Cerceris arenaria, Ammophila sabulosa, Crabro cribrarius, and Odynerus spinipes. Saunders writes for naturalists who want accurate, readable natural history. The book remains a charming guide to the stinging insects of Britain, their habits, nests, and lives.
33957-the-cabinet-minister-a-farce-in-fo:
Arthur W. Pinero wrote this farce in four acts, published in London in 1892 by William Heinemann, with an introductory note by Malcolm C. Salaman. Pinero held strong views on farce, claiming for it a wider scope and purpose than the old Adelphi farce or the newer Parisian kind. He argued that farce must grow into the modern form of comedy.

The play itself turns on a cabinet minister, his household, and the tangles of politics and society. Pinero writes with wit and stagecraft. The volume gives readers a key Pinero farce from his most fruitful years.
34061-the-earliest-electromagnetic-instr:
Robert A. Chipman wrote this Smithsonian paper on the earliest electromagnetic instruments, paper thirty-eight in Bulletin 240. The paper moves from electrostatic instruments before 1800 through voltaic and galvanic electricity from 1800 to 1820, then to Oersted's discovery and the start of electromagnetic work. Models of tools by Schweigger help the text.

Chipman weighs dates and first claims, and he sets out the first electromagnetic multipliers before he draws his conclusions. The paper lists early tools in order, and it tells how makers tried one form after another. It notes who came first and who came later. The work helps a reader see how a new field grew step by step, from plain tests to tools that could gauge a current.
34113-an-almanac-of-twelve-sports:
William Nicholson's An Almanac of Twelve Sports pairs a full calendar for 1898 with a sport for each month, in words by Rudyard Kipling. Hunting opens the year, and coursing, racing, boating, and fishing follow in turn.

Each month gets a short comic verse and a picture, poking fun at the sportsman as much as praising the sport. The book works as a calendar with wit, and as a small set of sporting pictures. Kipling's verses name old sporting writers, from Surtees to Jorrocks, as the sportsman's true company. The calendar keeps the true days of 1898, so the book served as a working year-book as well as a jest.
34184-magda-a-play-in-four-acts:
Hermann Sudermann wrote this play in four acts, translated from the German by Charles Edward Amory Winslow, with copyright in 1895 by Lamson, Wolffe and Company. Characters include Lieutenant-Colonel Leopold Schwartz, Pastor Heffterdingt, Doctor Von Kellner, Max, Major-General Von Klebs, Professor Beckmann, Mrs. Schwartz the stepmother, and sisters Magda, Marie, and Franziska.

The synopsis sets all four acts in the Schwartzs' home: afternoon, evening of the same day, the next morning, and the same morning. A note praises Sudermann's move from novels to drama and calls Heimat his masterpiece. Magda offers a tense family drama of a daughter's return.
3608-the-ragged-trousered-philanthropist:
Robert Tressell writes a socialist novel about house painters in the fictional town of Mugsborough, whose workers call themselves philanthropists because they labor to enrich their employers. Chapters include The Mysterious Stranger, The Financiers, The Placard, The Exterminating Machines, and The Wages of Intelligence. At the center stands Owen, a painter who tries to teach his mates why they stay poor.

Tressell describes the relations between workmen and employers, their lives at work and out of work, and their pleasures and hopes. His novel argues that workers produce all wealth yet receive only a fraction of it. The book became a classic of British labor literature and suits readers interested in socialism, craft labor, and Edwardian England.
3768-the-lamp-and-the-bell-a-drama-in-fi:
Edna Saint Vincent Millay wrote this verse drama for the fiftieth anniversary of the Vassar College Alumnae Association, and it was played by alumnae themselves. The action moves in an Italian Renaissance world of kings and dukes, where Lorenzo rules Fiori and Mario rules Lagoverde. At its heart stand two young women, Beatrice, called Rose-Red, and Bianca, called Snow-White, whose friendship outlasts courts, marriages, and wars.

The lamp and the bell of the title name what each means to the other. One is a flame the wind cannot blow out, and the other is a bell that tells a traveler she is near home. Millay writes in lyric verse that stays clear even in passion. Readers who like poetic drama will find a play about love between friends, rare on stage then and now, and tender without sentiment.
381-memories-and-portraits:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers personal essays in this volume, meant to be read straight through like a life in pieces. Childhood, college days, an old Scots gardener, the manse, and talks with friends fill the pages. Portraits of his father and grandfather sit beside musings on dogs, talk, and romance.

Stevenson says the thread that binds them is his own young face, glimpsed as if in a well. The tone is fond, frank, and at times sad for friends now gone. The book gives a rare self-portrait by indirection, through places and people who made the writer he became.
4029-true-stories-about-dogs-and-cats:
A book of true animal stories gathers plain tales of dogs and cats and the people who kept them. In one sampled tale, a pet cat who had lost all her kittens but one takes in strange young orphans. She carries them one by one to her nest and nurses them as her own.

Soon the old cat and her roguish adopted children range through every room of the house. Such stories favor kindness, pluck, and the odd wisdom of animals over fine writing. The book suits young readers and animal lovers, offering short, true anecdotes that can be read one at a time at bedtime or in class.
4038-imaginary-portraits:
Walter Horatio Pater's imaginary portraits sketch invented figures who feel truer than real people, set within a tree architecture of moss-grown balusters, statues, and fountains. The portraits group themselves with a fittingness no real life quite shows, lit by a light sought in vain on anything actual.

Windless afternoons hang over the scenes, and the narrator always expects rain by evening, as storms gather beyond the garden calm. Pater uses these figures to test ideas about art, faith, and character. Readers who enjoy prose portraits and quiet speculation will find a book of strange, polished beauty.
4216-touch-and-go-a-play-in-three-acts:
D. H. Lawrence's play Touch and Go, in three acts, follows Oliver, Anabel, and Gerald through a friendship turned to bitterness. Oliver speaks bitterly of Gerald's sneering attitude in the deepest things, and of a passion that has cooled to something almost casual.

Anabel answers that she was awfully fond of Oliver, trusted him, and trusts him still, knowing how fond Gerald was of him. Lawrence writes the triangle in plain, charged speech, where love, work, and class collide. Readers who like modern drama of feeling will find a short, intense play.
4243-sir-thomas-more-or-colloquies-on-th:
Robert Southey first published these dialogues in 1824. Their full title was Sir Thomas More, or Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society. The present volume reprints a selection from an 1887 Cassell edition. In them Southey talks with the ghost of Thomas More. Their subject is how society changes and where it may be heading.

The chosen colloquies treat the chief rules of social life. They show Southey as he saw those principles late in life. One pleasant piece portrays the author himself among his books. Some topical pieces were left out, but the dialogues keep their mix of hope and doubt.
447-maggie-a-girl-of-the-streets:
Stephen Crane tells of Maggie Johnson, a girl raised in the slums of New York, in this stark early novel. Rum Alley fights, a drunken mother, and a brutal brother shape her youth. When a bartender named Pete courts her with fine clothes and music halls, Maggie dreams of escape from the tenement.

Crane writes in short, hard scenes, with dialect speech and a cold eye for poverty's traps. Hope curdles fast, and the streets claim Maggie in the end. The novel shocked readers of its day and now stands as a landmark of American realism, unsparing yet full of pity for its heroine.
4497-the-sentimentalists:
George Meredith left this comedy unfinished, under the title The Sentimentalists. Its persons include Homeware, Professor Spiral, Arden in love with Astraea, Swithin the sympathetic, Osier, Dame Dresden sister to Homeware, Astraea her niece, Lyra a wife, Lady Oldlace, Virginia, and Winifred. The scene is a Surrey garden in early summer.

It is set outdoors in Surrey, in early summer, among tall boxwood hedges, a stage for talk, sentiment, and comedy of manners. Meredith's unfinished play shows his late interest in sentiment itself: how feeling is performed, praised, and mocked. Readers get a fragment, charming in itself, and a glimpse of a comedy its author did not live to finish.
4514-tales-of-men-and-ghosts:
Edith Wharton published Tales of Men and Ghosts in London in 1910, gathering ten stories that mix the supernatural with social life. The contents run from The Bolted Door and His Father's Son through The Daunt Diana, The Debt, and Full Circle, to The Legend, The Eyes, The Blond Beast, Afterward, and The Letters. Each tale sets a polished, well-mannered world against something uncanny or unresolved.

Wharton's ghosts are often less frightening than the guilt, greed, or pride of the living people who meet them. A murder concealed, a debt unpaid, or a letter kept too long can haunt a character more surely than any spirit. Readers get finely written ghost stories for adults, where manners hide sharp moral choices, and where the past refuses to stay buried.
4764-a-family-man-in-three-acts:
John Galsworthy wrote A Family Man as a play in three acts, in the fifth series of his plays. Its characters include John Builder, of Builder and Builder, his wife Julia, and daughters Athene and Maud. Ralph Builder, John's brother and partner, Guy Herringhame, a flying man, and Annie, a young person in blue, also appear, with Camille, Mrs. Builder's French maid, and Topping, Builder's manservant.

The mayor of Breconridge, his secretary Harris, and Francis Chantrey, a justice, round out the cast. Moon, a constable, Martin, a police sergeant, a journalist from The Comet, a poacher's figure, and voices of small boys complete it. Action passes in Breconridge, in the Midlands, from Builder's study after breakfast to a studio, then to Builder's study at lunchtime, and to the mayor's study the following day. Readers get a Galsworthy domestic drama about a strong-willed family man and those who resist him.
5352-marjorie-s-three-gifts:
Louisa M. Alcott's Marjorie's Three Gifts opens with Marjorie shelling peas on a doorstep, roses peeping through the porch lattice, and wind playing in her curly hair. Sunshine turns her faded gingham to a golden gown. Old Rover lies at her feet, a white kitten purrs on her shoulder, and robins hop about chirping a happy birthday.

Alcott, author of Little Women, writes a short birthday story of a girl, her pets, and three gifts that teach kindness and gratitude. The book offers young readers a warm, old-fashioned tale, published in Boston in 1899, in the manner of Alcott's best stories for children.
5605-the-power-of-movement-in-plants:
Charles Darwin, assisted by his son Francis Darwin, wrote The Power of Movement in Plants as a study of how plants move. The contents run from circumnutating movements of seedlings through sensitivity of the root tip to contact. They cover mature plants, climbing plants, sleep movements of leaves and cotyledons, and movements excited by light and gravitation, ending with concluding remarks.

Darwin shows seedlings bending, roots feeling their way, leaves folding at night, and stems climbing, all through small, steady motions. Readers get a classic of plant science, careful, experimental, and full of observation. It remains a landmark for anyone curious about how plants sense their world.
5735-the-valley-of-the-giants:
Peter Kyne sets The Valley of the Giants in California in the summer of 1850, opening as a topsail schooner slips into a cove under Trinidad Head. A man lands with a long squirrel rifle, an axe, and a brown canvas pack of food and clothing, watches the small boat return, and steps into the redwood country. From that landing, the novel grows into a lumber saga of giant trees, claims, and rivalries.

You get a big, vigorous adventure of the early West, where forests are both wealth and wonder. Kyne writes with energy about work, risk, and the men who measured themselves against trees larger than houses. The book suits fans of western and lumber fiction, and readers who enjoy a story that opens quietly on a beach before widening into a fight for a valley.
5806-the-pot-boiler-a-comedy-in-four-act:
Upton Sinclair writes about writing itself in The Pot Boiler, a comedy in four acts edited by Haldeman Julius. Its real play characters include Will, the author, Peggy, joint author and critic, Bill, their eight-year-old son, and Dad, among others. The comedy turns on a household trying to produce a potboiler, a book written quickly to sell, while art, money, and family pride collide.

Readers and theatre groups will find Sinclair in a lighter mood, mocking literary commerce without losing sympathy for writers. The play-within-a-play structure lets arguments about art happen as jokes and quarrels. It suits those who enjoy Sinclair beyond his novels, and anyone who has wondered what happens when a writer must please both muse and market.
5987-in-kedar-s-tents:
Henry Seton Merriman sets a tale of sowing and reaping that moves from Ronda and a Moorish garden to Madrid and Toledo. The chapters promise contraband, a love letter, a war of wit, a tangled web, and a cross-examination, with priestcraft, swordcraft, and womancraft weighed in turn.

One sows and another reaps, and the road runs through cities of discontent and strife toward midnight, dawn, and at last the dawn of peace. Merriman blends romance with intrigue across Spain. Concepción takes the road, Larralde names his price, and honor is tested before the end.
5996-essays-on-russian-novelists:
William Lyon Phelps opens with Russia humbled by the Japanese war, her navy destroyed, armies beaten, treasury drained, and pride laid in dust. He argues that a nation's greatness lies not in battleships or wealth, but in intellectual splendor, in ideas given to the world, and in gifts to literature and art.

The essays that follow read Russian fiction as a window on national character. Phelps invites American readers, proud of industrial power, to weigh their own gifts against Russia's in literature and music. The book treats novels as evidence of a people's inner life, not mere entertainment.
6117-success-with-small-fruits:
E. P. Roe dedicates Success with Small Fruits to Charles Downing, neighbor, friend, and horticulturist, from whom he hopes to keep learning. His preface says a book should be judged by what it attempts, and this volume aims to lure men and women back to their original calling, that of gardening.

Roe imagines Eve helping Adam, especially as the sun declined, with small fruits for breakfast, dinner, and supper, and perhaps between meals. Even mortals who have sinned more than once can fare as well, he says. The Adams and Eves of every generation can have an Eden if they wish, and Eve often creates it.
634-miscellaneous-mathematical-constants:
Simon Plouffe collects high-precision values of mathematical constants in this reference volume, drawn from a Simon Fraser University index. Artin's constant, the Backhouse constant, Catalan's constant, Champernowne's constant, and dozens more appear, many to thousands of digits. Cosine, cube roots, gamma values, and Feigenbaum numbers share the store.

The book serves workers who need true digits to test code or theory, not casual readers. Its tables, gathered with Plouffe's permission, keep a public record of numbers that recur across math and physics. For the curious it stands as a quiet monument to how much order hides in a few strange digits.
6347-hobson-s-choice-a-lancashire-comedy:
Harold Brighouse's Lancashire comedy in four acts was first produced in America, then in London at the Apollo Theatre on June 22, 1916. Henry Horatio Hobson, bootmaker, rules three daughters, Alice, Maggie, and Vickey, with a strap and a temper, while Will Mossop, his boot hand, loves Maggie and she does the taking up. Hobson lifts a trap, calls Will up, and declares he cannot leather a lass, being female and exempt, but he can leather him.

The cast list names Lydia Bilbrooke, Edyth Goodall, and Hilda Davies as the daughters, Norman McKinnel as Hobson, and Joe Nightingale as Mossop. Brighouse writes Lancashire speech with comic precision, as Maggie, the cleverest Hobson, turns her father's shop and his choice against him. The play is a battle of wills in a boot shop, where a daughter's choice proves the best business of all.
6399-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
After twelve emperors, Suetonius adds lives of poets: Terence, Juvenal, Persius, Horace, Lucan, and Pliny. Terence, Publius Terentius Afer, a native of Carthage, was a slave at Rome of Senator Terentius Lucanus. Struck by his abilities and handsome person, the senator gave him a liberal education and freedom at maturity. Some call him a war captive, but Fenestella shows his birth and death fell between the second and third Punic wars, when no such capture could have happened.

Terence lived familiarly with men of high station, and his comedies won Roman favour. A later poet in the set dies soon after honourable banishment as prefect of a cohort on Egypt's far frontier. The punishment was chosen as severe enough for a venial, droll offence, and he was worn down by grief and weariness of life. Suetonius gives literary lives with the same anecdotal care as imperial ones, in Thomson's translation.
6680-the-bores-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Molière's The Bores, first played in August 1661, is a character comedy where the pests are not one or two leads, but a parade of figures. Each bore enters, performs a brief role, and leaves, strung on a weak thread of talk by an unwilling listener. The note that opens the text calls the method less artful, yet natural, a set of tableaux more than a plot.

Monologues, not situations, carry the fun, as each new bore shows a fresh folly. Molière's verse keeps the parade brisk. The Bores is a lively, if loose, early comedy, best enjoyed as a gallery of human pests, one after another.
6706-the-emancipation-of-massachusetts:
Brooks Adams traces Massachusetts from a theocratic commonwealth toward emancipation, in dream and in reality. His prefatory note thanks Mellen Chamberlain, Charles Deane, and Frank Cushing, whose unpublished Zuñi research aided the work, along with William James and others. Faults, Adams says, are his own; any merit belongs to his helpers.

Chapters on the commonwealth, the Antinomians, and the Cambridge Platform lead into a long struggle for religious and political freedom. Adams writes as a bold, opinionated historian, keen on the clash of ideas. The Emancipation of Massachusetts is a sharp, classic study of New England's break with old rule.
6861-vautrin-a-drama-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's Vautrin was first played at the Porte-Saint-Martin in Paris in March 1840. It opens with an author's preface. Balzac writes on the difficulty of writing about his own play five days after its first night. Every spectator, Balzac says, has written his own preface, and his single voice will seem inferior to so many divergent ones. A cannon's report, he jokes, is never so effective as fireworks.

Must he explain his work, complain of the ban that delayed it, or name its only true commentator, the actor Lemaitre? Balzac leaves the play to speak. Vautrin is a bold, historic drama of a master criminal, written by a novelist at his peak.
6992-belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-act:
A A Milne's Belinda, an April folly in three acts, was produced by Dion Boucicault at the New Theatre in London on April 8, 1918. The cast lists Irene Vanbrugh as Belinda Tremayne, Isabel Elsom as her daughter Delia, Boucicault as Harold Baxter, and Dennis Neilson Terry as Claude Devenish. John Tremayne and Betty complete the household, and the action sits in Belinda's country house in Devonshire at the end of April.

The first act plays in the garden, the second and last in the hall, on a lovely April afternoon that foretastes summer. Betty, a middle aged servant, fastens a hammock to a tree as the play opens, with a garden table and chairs set for talk. Milne writes a light comedy of love, pride, and spring folly in three brisk acts.
7084-a-girl-among-the-anarchists:
Isabel Meredith writes A Girl Among the Anarchists with a preface owning the courage needed to write on anarchism even with clinical sympathy or scientific detachment. Anarchists, she argues, are curiously interesting and much in need of observation, since leading article quacks show no insight into them as phenomenon, portent, or disease. Read with understanding, the book will show how anarchism grows endemic in Western civilizations as cholera is endemic in India.

Meredith, once a humble member of a newspaper staff, writes from inside knowledge of the movement's circles. The girl of the title moves among exiles, plotters, and idealists, learning their hopes and their follies. The book is a novel of political passion, told by one who watched it close at hand.
7239-men-women-and-boats:
Stephen Crane's Men, Women, and Boats gathers tales and sketches from out-of-print volumes and old magazine files, edited with an introduction by Vincent Starrett. Some pieces appear here for the first time between covers, and some for the first time in this country, rescued from scattered print. The Open Boat, one of Crane's finest stories, anchors the book by permission of its holders.

Starrett notes with regret that The Blue Hotel had to be left out for copyright reasons, a gap the editor marks rather than hides. The stories that remain show Crane's sharp eye for people under pressure, at sea and on land. This collection gives a fuller, fairer view of a short, brilliant career.
7258-dreams-waking-thoughts-and-incident:
William Beckford's Dreams, Waking Thoughts, and Incidents travels Europe in a series of letters. It opens on June 19, 1780, with a rare confession: shall he tell his correspondent his dreams, since giving an account of his time is little better?? A frequent mist hovers before his eyes, he writes, so that colours and forms delude him through a hazy medium.

Beckford owns himself a more ideal being than most travellers, and his letters mix dream, waking fancy, and incident without apology. The wise may scoff at such a guide, he admits, yet his correspondents reap vivid pictures of outlandish countries all the same. The book reads as a young man's grand tour through a mind half in dream.
7310-mr-pim-passes-by-a-comedy-in-three-:
A. A. Milne's Mr Pim Passes By is a comedy in three acts, set in the morning-room at Marden House, Buckinghamshire, on a day in July. George Marden, justice of the peace, his wife Olivia, his niece Dinah, his aunt Lady Marden, Brian Strange, and the visitor Carraway Pim make up the cast, with Anne in service. The play lists its original casts at Manchester's Gaiety and London's New Theatre.

Milne builds farce from a chance caller whose talk threatens a settled marriage, letting wit and misunderstanding do the work of plot. The comedy stays light, civilised, and brisk, with each act tightening the knot before it slips loose. Readers get a stage piece that plays as well on the page.
7432-on-nothing-kindred-subjects:
Hilaire Belloc dedicated these essays to Maurice Baring, and their subject is announced in the title: nothing, and kindred subjects. The contents wander as Belloc's mind wandered. He writes on taking up one's pen, and on getting respected in inns and hotels. He writes on ignorance, on advertisement, and on a house. He writes on a dog and a man, and also on tea. Railways, conversations in trains, and the return of the dead all get their turn.

Later essays grow sharper, touching national debts, lords, and jingoes in the shape of a warning. But the tone stays that of a man talking after dinner, serious about small things and playful about great ones. Readers who know The Path to Rome will recognize the same voice here, looser and more mischievous, enjoying the freedom of having nothing in particular to prove.
753-arizona-nights:
Stewart Edward White wrote these tales of Arizona nights, when cowboys, miners, and travellers gather round fires and swap stories. The desert by night is the real hero: cool air, bright stars, and the long quiet after a day's hard riding. Each tale grows from a campfire yarn, told in the drawl of men who lived the life.

White knew the Southwest at first hand, and his prose carries its dust, heat, and humour. The stories praise courage and good fellowship without hiding the risks of frontier life. The book helped fix the image of Arizona in the American mind, and it still reads as a warm, authentic set of western tales.
7765-night-must-fall-a-play-in-three-act:
Emlyn Williams's Night Must Fall, a play in three acts, takes place in the sitting room of Forest Corner, Mrs. Bramson's Essex bungalow, in the present day. The cast lists the Lord Chief Justice, Mrs. Bramson, her niece Olivia Grayne, Hubert Laurie, Nurse Libby, cook Mrs. Terence, maid Dora, and Inspector Belsize.

Act One opens on an October morning, later scenes follow twelve days and two days on, ending at nightfall. Performing rights rest with the author's agent, Walter Peacock of Haymarket. The play builds dread in a quiet house, where charm may hide a killer.
7999-the-bible-king-james-version-comple:
Despite its title, the text hosted here runs from Genesis through the early chapters of 2 Chronicles, in the King James Version. It opens with creation, follows the patriarchs, the Exodus, the wilderness years, and the conquest, then traces Israel's judges and kings from Saul and David through Solomon. The run ends in the reign of Rehoboam, with Shishak of Egypt carrying off the treasures of the temple and the king's house.

Read as a continuous narrative, the volume carries the Bible's first great arc: a people chosen, delivered, settled, and divided. Its verse-numbered text suits steady, consecutive reading from the beginning. Readers should note the scope as it stands, since later books of the Bible are not included in this file.
8044-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Acts, the second volume addressed to Theophilus, picks up where Luke's Gospel ends, with Jesus risen and speaking of the kingdom for forty days. From Pentecost in Jerusalem, the story spreads outward: Peter preaches, Stephen is stoned, Philip meets an Ethiopian official. Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle, and Paul carries the message through Asia Minor and Greece to Rome itself.
