Luke writes Acts as a travel story and a church history in one, full of speeches, shipwrecks, trials, and escapes. It explains how a small Jewish sect became a movement across the Roman world. In the King James Version, its pace and drama make it the most readable history in the New Testament, and the bridge between the Gospels and the letters.
8079-pamela-giraud-a-play-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's play Pamela Giraud was first performed in Paris at the Théâtre de la Gaîté on September 26, 1843. Its persons include General de Verby, Dupré the lawyer, the merchant Rousseau and his son Jules. The porter Giraud, and Pamela Giraud herself, an artificial flower-maker whose attic workshop opens the first act. The scene is Paris during the Napoleonic plots under Louis XVIII, between 1815 and 1824.

The play turns on love, family pride, and political conspiracy, with police, magistrates, and gendarmes moving through its intrigues. Balzac, better known as a novelist, shows here his stagecraft and his eye for Parisian social types. For readers of his fiction, the play is a fascinating side piece, and a chance to see his characters speak rather than narrate.
8125-impressions-and-comments:
Havelock Ellis gathered these impressions and comments from notes made on random leaves over many years, on things in life and thought that chanced to strike his attention. His preface compares the notes to autumn leaves: having served their use, they no longer need to cling to the tree, so let them be scattered to the winds. He warns that such leaves cannot be judged as though they formed a book, since they are fragments, not a system.

The pieces range across psychology, literature, sex, society, and morals, in the voice of a humane and curious observer. Ellis, best known for his studies of human sexuality, here shows his wider mind. The book rewards dipping in at random, and it gives a candid portrait of an Edwardian thinker thinking aloud.
8196-under-the-skylights:
Henry Blake Fuller collected three stories under the skylights, with a prefatory note explaining that the final section. On Dr Gowdy and the squash, is reprinted by permission from Harper's Magazine, while the rest appears for the first time. The contents are The Downfall of Abner Joyce, Little O'Grady versus the Grindstone, and Dr Gowdy and the Squash. The first story opens with Abner Joyce taking a place in literature at once, when his first book, This Weary World, made readers feel fiction richer by one vital book.

Fuller's stories examine literary ambition, Chicago life, and the comedy of artistic failure. His prose is polished and ironic, in the manner of the American realist novel. For readers of Fuller and of Chicago fiction, the collection offers three sharp, well-made tales, and a portrait of authorship itself.
8202-sermons-on-national-subjects:
Charles Kingsley published Sermons on National Subjects in a first edition of 1880, reprinted in 1886 and again in this Macmillan edition of 1890. Its sermons begin with The King of the Earth, Holy Scripture, and The Kingdom of God, continue through Christmas, true abstinence, Good Friday. Easter, the Comforter, Whit Sunday, and Ascension Day, and include The Fount of Science and three sermons on the cholera. The subjects are national because Kingsley preached them as a citizen as well as a clergyman.

Kingsley argues that faith should speak to public life: to science, to sickness, and to the nation's duties. His preaching is vigorous, direct, and socially engaged, in the manner of the Christian Socialist movement he helped lead. For readers of Victorian religion, the volume shows a famous preacher addressing his country's crises from the pulpit.
8271-the-world-english-bible-web-acts:
Acts continues Luke's story after Jesus' resurrection, following his followers from Jerusalem out across the Roman world. The Holy Spirit falls on the apostles at Pentecost, Peter preaches to crowds, and the church grows amid arrests and miracles. Stephen's death scatters believers, and the gospel reaches Samaritans, an Ethiopian official, and a Roman officer.

The second half belongs to Paul: his conversion on the road to Damascus, three missionary journeys, shipwreck, and a final appeal in Rome. Acts is the church's earliest history, written with a storyteller's pace. Readers get both a travel narrative and an account of how a small Jewish sect became a movement spanning an empire.
839-new-arabian-nights:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these tales of London adventure in the manner of the Arabian Nights, where chance meetings lead to danger and romance. The Suicide Club opens the set, with a young man drawn into a secret society, and the Rajah's Diamond follows, with a stolen gem passing from hand to hand.

Stevenson writes with dash and wit, turning foggy streets into a stage for princes, doctors, and rogues. The tales are short, brisk, and full of surprise, and they show the young author finding his voice. The book delights readers who enjoy romance with a modern, urban twist, told by a master storyteller.
8397-expositions-of-holy-scripture-the-a:
Alexander MacLaren, the great Baptist preacher of Manchester, wrote these expositions on the Acts of the Apostles, chapters 1 to 12, verse by verse. Contents move from the Ascension and the forty days to Pentecost, the apostolic witnesses, and the growth of the Jerusalem church, with each passage turned into a sermon-length meditation.

MacLaren's method is textual and pastoral: he opens a verse, draws out its meaning, and presses it home to daily conduct. Generations of preachers kept his expositions on their desks as a model of clear, warm preaching. Readers get not a commentary for scholars, but sermons for the pew, grounded in the text and aimed at the heart.
841-men-women-and-ghosts:
Amy Lowell wrote these poems on men, women, and ghosts, in the free, vivid style that made her a leader of Imagism. The poems take small scenes, a room, a garden, a face, and let them grow into portraits of longing, pride, and loss. Ghosts here are memories as much as spirits, haunting the living.

Lowell writes with a painter's eye for colour and a musician's ear for rhythm, breaking lines to suit the thought. The collection shows her range, from tender lyrics to sharp character sketches. It remains a key volume for readers of modern American poetry, and for those who like verse that sees clearly and feels deeply.
8432-black-rebellion-five-slave-revolts:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson gathers five slave revolts in Black Rebellion, drawn from his Travellers and Outlaws, with an appendix of authorities. A transcriber's note confirms the five chapters are commonly called by this title, and Higginson's author's note frames episodes in American history where enslaved people rose against their bondage.

Higginson, an abolitionist minister and colonel of a Black regiment in the Civil War, wrote with sympathy for the rebels and care for sources. Readers get five episodes of resistance, told as history rather than romance. The book remains an early, important attempt to center enslaved people's agency in American history, written by a man who had fought beside them.
8599-fairy-tales-from-the-arabian-nights:
E. Dixon edited this first series of tales from the Arabian Nights, using the 1821 Galland text, lightly shortened for young readers. The selection opens with Persian princes and princesses of the sea, then moves through princes Ahmed and Camaralzaman, the story of Zobeide, and the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor. Each tale is told plainly, with the marvels left intact and the framing kept short.

Sinbad's seven voyages, full of strange islands, giant birds, and narrow escapes, anchor the second half of the book. Around them sit love stories, lost talismans, and fairy helpers, all in the Nights' familiar mix of adventure and moral turn. The volume suits readers meeting these tales for the first time, and it shows how Victorian editors shaped an old story collection for the nursery and the schoolroom.
8606-the-blue-bird-a-fairy-play-in-six-a:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote this fairy play about two poor children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, sent to find the Blue Bird of happiness, in Alexander Teixeira de Mattos's translation. A fairy sets them travelling with Light as their guide, while the dog, cat, bread, sugar, fire, water, and milk all take human shape and talk. Dead grandparents, Night, Time, and the Luxuries join the huge cast.

Across six acts the children visit the Land of Memory, the Palace of Night, and the Kingdom of the Future, always missing the bird they seek. The play's point lands at home: happiness was near all along, in kindness and in seeing familiar things with fresh eyes. Staged worldwide since its first success, it remains a gentle, strange fable that works for children on stage and for adults reading it as poetry.
8732-through-the-fray-a-tale-of-the-ludd:
G. A. Henty sets this tale in Marsden, Yorkshire, in 1807, where boys stream out of Mr Hathorn's academy at one o'clock in knee breeches and stiff, flat-topped caps. The schoolroom scene fixes a vanished England before the story moves into the Luddite riots, when textile workers smashed the machines they blamed for their hunger. A fishing expedition opens the book, but the fray soon claims its hero.

Through the hero's eyes, readers meet mill owners, workers, soldiers, and secret oath-bound bands, and learn how fear and anger spread through mill towns. Henty, writing for boys, sides with order while showing the workers' grievances plainly enough to follow. The novel gives a vivid, if partisan, introduction to one of Britain's first industrial conflicts, and to the world of early factories that made it.
8733-the-hermits:
Charles Kingsley tells the lives of the early Christian hermits in this 1891 Macmillan volume, first printed in parts in 1868. An introduction leads into Saint Antony, Paul the first hermit, Hilarion, and Arsenius, then the hermits of Asia, Basil, and Simeon Stylites on his pillar. Hermits of Europe follow, with Severinus, apostle of Noricum, the Celtic hermits, and Saint Malo, among others, and a picture of Saint Brendan setting sail.

Kingsley, clergyman and novelist, treats solitude as both heroic and strange, admiring the hermits' discipline while noting its excesses. The lives mix legend, history, and moral reflection, drawn from ancient sources retold for Victorian readers. Students of early Christianity will find a readable introduction to desert and island asceticism. General readers a set of vivid, sometimes startling portraits of men and women who fled the world to find God.
8832-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's Acts opens as a sequel: Luke's former narrative, addressed to Theophilus, dealt with all Jesus did and taught as a beginning. Down to the day he was taken up to Heaven after instructing his chosen apostles through the Holy Spirit. After suffering, Jesus showed himself alive with many sure proofs, appearing at intervals during forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God. He charged the apostles not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promised gift.

John baptized with water, Jesus says, but before many days pass they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. The story that follows carries the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome. Weymouth's plain English keeps Acts' travel, speeches, and conflicts moving briskly. Readers get the early Church's story whole, from Pentecost to Paul's house arrest, in a translation built for clarity rather than grandeur.
9374-a-knight-of-the-nets:
Amelia Barr wrote this fishing-village novel in 1896, set in Pittendurie, a place in Fife few travelers ever find. Grey sky and brown waters open the tale, as the narrator's heart flies back to northern seas and the winter rose of northern skies. Christina and Andrew lead the story, through an ailing heart and the lash of the whip.

A lost bride, a question of money, and a great deliverance follow, with the little Sophy near the end. Barr writes of fisherfolk with sympathy and grit. The novel remains a sturdy, romantic tale of the Scottish coast, its work, faith, and love.
9466-the-quest-of-happy-hearts:
Kathleen Hay wrote The Quest of Happy Hearts, a girls' tale of a visit to a great old house at Land's End. Nora and her friends, sent off while their father is away on business, face the trip with gloom. Their great-aunt Janice Meredith waits at a house set on the edge of a forest. What starts as a dull duty soon turns into a quest, with a tower room at its heart.

Chapters follow plans, forest walks, a party, and the tale of the tower room itself, as the girls add to their quest day by day. Marty and Jerry join the fun, and old secrets lend the house charm. A reader gets a warm, old-style girls' adventure, full of friendship, mystery, and the joy of a strange house explored.
9825-a-calendar-of-sonnets:
Helen Jackson, an American poet, arranged these sonnets by the months of the year, opening with January in 1886. Each poem takes one month's weather and mood, from winter's frozen pulse to summer roses and autumn quiet.

The sonnets are short, formal, and musical, and they ask readers to notice small changes: ice on streams, first warmth, harvest light, and the year's slow turn. Jackson keeps her language plain and her images close to nature. The little book works as a year in verse, meant to be read one month at a time, slowly, through all four seasons.
9838-strong-hearts:
George W. Cable wrote Strong Hearts in 1899, a book of tales on one principle, told three or four times over. Contents list The Solitary, The Taxidermist, and The Entomologist, with The Solitary first printed as Gregory's Island. Cable likens his tripled tale to Pharaoh's doubled dream: a thing established. Each story sets heroic natures and poetic fates to one universal truth.

The tales follow strong hearts through solitude, craft, and science, with Cable's Louisiana warmth. His prose favors moral poetry over mere plot. A reader gets a thoughtful set of linked stories, where courage proves itself in varied lives.
a-book-of-quaker-saints: Lucy Violet Hodgkin tells the lives of Quaker saints for young readers. Her chapters include the shepherd of Pendle Hill, the angel of Beverley, and the man in leather breeches. Each life shows steadfast faith, plain speech, and courage under trial in story form. The book presents these figures as models of a simple and faithful life.
a-brief-bible-history-a-survey-of-the-ol:
A Brief Bible History, published in 1922 by James Oscar Boyd and J Gresham Machen, surveys the history of the Old and New Testaments. The book presents that history as the story of God's redeeming grace. Its chapters trace the stream of God's redeeming purposes flowing down through the older, Old Testament times.

The survey then follows the same purpose broadening and deepening in the New Testament, in Jesus Christ and his Church. Boyd and Machen wrote as Bible teachers, and the book reads as a clear, ordered introduction for students. It gives readers the whole arc of scripture in brief compass, from the first histories to the early church, in one connected account.
a-calendar-of-sonnets: Helen Hunt Jackson writes a calendar of sonnets that follows the months of the year. Each poem takes its season as a theme, from winter snow and patient roses to summer streams and autumn fires. The verses link nature with love, loss, and the inner life in measured sonnet form. The collection offers a poem for the turning year, month by month.
a-catechism-of-familiar-things-their-his: This anonymous catechism explains familiar things, their history, and how they were discovered. In question and answer form it treats dew, rain, wind, lightning, corn, tea, coffee, cotton, wool, and many other everyday subjects. A short account of natural phenomena accompanies the history of each thing. Enlarged for schools and families, the book turns common objects into lessons in science and history.
a-family-man-in-three-acts:
A Family Man is a play in three acts by John Galsworthy, published in 1922. Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright, viewed as one of the first writers of the Edwardian era, who challenged the ideals of the society that Victorian literature before him had depicted. He later won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and his Forsyte Saga became his most famous work.

On stage, this play puts a family man at the center of domestic tension. Galsworthy's drama typically sets private comfort against public duty and respectability, and A Family Man works that ground in three acts. The printed play preserves a piece of his Edwardian theatre, from the years when his stage work stood beside his novels in reputation.
a-girl-among-the-anarchists:
Isabel Meredith wrote A Girl Among the Anarchists from inside the London anarchist world she describes, and a preface by Morley Roberts insists that nothing in it is invented. The narrator tells her own story in the first person, beginning with a strange childhood and her arrival among the exiles, printers, and speakers of the movement.

Chapters follow a police scare, a rescue, the office of the paper called the Tocsin, and the escape of a dynamitard. Portraits of anarchist personalities sit beside meetings, flights, and quarrels over what the cause demands. The closing chapters bring a crisis and the last toll of the Tocsin, leaving a rare insider picture of a feared and mostly peaceful circle.
a-knight-of-the-nets: Amelia Barr writes a knight of the nets in a story of northern seas and hearts. Chapters follow Christina and Andrew through an ailing heart, the lash of the whip, and a lost bride. Questions of money, deliverance, and the righting of a wrong drive the plot. Barr sets her tale against grey skies and brown waters.
a-librarian-s-open-shelf-essays-on-vario: Arthur Elmore Bostwick opens a librarian's shelf of essays on various subjects. His pieces ask whether readers read, what makes people read, and how book titles change. Selective education, the uses of fiction, and modern education follow. Bostwick writes for librarians and book lovers about reading and libraries. Book lovers will enjoy these short talks on reading and libraries.
a-list-of-factorial-math-constants: A bare reference table of factorials, computed once by a simple Scheme program whose source code has been lost, as the file's own note explains. It gives every factorial from 1! through 99!, then jumps by hundreds to 900! and by thousands to 10,000!, printing each full value with its digit count. There is no prose beyond the heading notes. The file serves as ready-made big-number data for checking arithmetic, testing software, or satisfying curiosity about how fast factorials grow.
a-philological-essay-concerning-the-pygm: Edward Tyson examines the pygmies of ancient legend in this philological essay, newly edited with an introduction by Bertram Windle. Drawing on De Quatrefage's monograph and on facts gathered from other published sources, he brings forward tales chosen to establish his points about these small peoples of myth. The essay makes no claim to exhaust its literature, offering selected evidence rather than a complete survey.
acetaria-a-discourse-of-sallets: John Evelyn writes Acetaria, a discourse of sallets, in this reprint of the first edition of 1699, issued by the Women's Auxiliary of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden in 1937. The edition corrects a few typographical errors and incorporates the author's errata. It keeps the old-style S of the original. The Latin and Greek sprinkled through the treatise mark its author as a man of letters, praising salads as the first subject of his second volume of a garden manual.
airship-wave-1896-1897-press-accounts:
Seventeen newspaper pieces from 1896 and 1897 make up The Great Airship Wave of 1896-1897, drawn from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America scans. Reports from Sacramento, Oakland, San Francisco, and San Jose open the scare in November 1896. By April 1897 the wave rolled over Kansas, Omaha, and Chicago, with inventors claiming the sky craft as their own.

Editors argued, witnesses swore, and hoaxers confessed in the columns reprinted here word for word. Nothing real was ever found, which makes the papers themselves the true record. The set preserves the primary evidence of America's first great mystery-airship panic, decades before flying saucers.
albertus-magnus-admirables-secrets:
Secrets ascribed to Albert the Great fill this French chapbook of natural magic, in a 1729 printing. Recipes, charms, and wonders of nature promise help with health, love, luck, and beasts. For two centuries it ranked among France's most popular books of hidden knowledge among common folk.

Herbs, stones, and household tricks mix with spells and signs in its pages. Scholars doubt the great Albert wrote a word of it himself. That hardly mattered to the buyers who treasured its lore. The book opens a window on popular belief, where folk magic and medieval science blend without a seam.
an-english-garner-critical-essays-litera: Edward Arber gathers an English garner of critical essays and literary fragments, with an introduction by J. Churton Collins. The volume collects short pieces of English criticism and letters that illumine authors and their times. Arber's garnering preserves scraps that would otherwise be lost to general readers. The fragments repay a slow, browsing read.
anthology-of-massachusetts-poets:
William Stanley Braithwaite gathers the poets of Massachusetts into one anthology, arranged by author. The contents open with Joseph Auslander's Home Bound and Katherine Lee Bates's America the Beautiful and Yellow Clover. Gamaliel Bradford, Alice Brown, Grace Hazard Conkling, and the child poet Hilda Conkling all appear in the early pages.

The poems run from formal odes and sonnets to short lyrics on war, faith, gardens, and Boston streets. Braithwaite, himself a poet and the era's best-known anthologist of new verse, aimed to represent his state's living poetry rather than its classics alone. The book works as a snapshot of New England verse at the moment he made it.
arizona-nights:
Stewart Edward White gathers Western tales told in the voice of men who worked cattle country in Arizona. The table of contents names stories about rustlers, drives, branding, Texas Rangers, buried treasure, and a two-gun man. A storm over the mesas opens the first tale, and the dry land shapes every scene that follows.

The tales move between camp talk and longer linked stories, ending with a long section called The Rawhide. White writes plain speech, hard riding, and desert weather with the ease of a man who knew ranch life. The book preserves the talk and habits of the old Southwest cattle frontier.
artist-and-public-and-other-essays-on-ar: Kenyon Cox writes essays on the artist and the public, on Millet, Raphael, and Saint Gaudens, and on the American school. He defends craft, design, and tradition against what he calls the illusion of progress, and he judges new painting by old standards of form. Illustrations of Millet works anchor the talk in pictures readers can study. Cox speaks as a painter critic, direct, firm, and sure of his taste.
balfour-taoist-texts:
Frederic Henry Balfour gathered his Taoist Texts in English in 1884. His anthology sorts the writings by morals, rule, and deep thought. Victorian readers met the philosophy of the Way through books like this.

Short pieces from the Taoist tradition speak in Balfour's clear English. They teach softness over force, quiet rule, and scorn for mere show. Laozi's heirs prize the still mind above wealth and loud fame. Balfour's picks favor calm wisdom over magic and cult practice here. The book stands as an early Western window into Taoist thought and ethics. Its quiet counsel still speaks past its Victorian frame to readers.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-03-ancie:
John Lord's third Beacon Lights volume surveys ancient achievements, beginning with governments and laws. Greek and Roman law gets a long, ordered account. Lycurgus and Solon come first, then the Athenian Ecclesia and Rome's struggle between patricians and plebeians. The Twelve Tables lead to the great jurists and Justinian's Code, Pandects, and Institutes. Marriage, paternal power, slavery, and personal rights are all weighed.

Arts and crafts fill the later lectures. Egyptian bronze vases show great skill in compounding metals, highly polished, with knives and daggers springing like steel. Wilkinson's surprise at porcelain vessels, rich in colour and beautiful in shape, is quoted with admiration, one bowl in the British Museum singled out. Lord builds a Victorian progress report on the ancient world: law first, then the arts that law protected.
beasts-and-super-beasts:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, gathered Beasts and Super-Beasts in 1914, a book of short stories famous for their polish and bite. Saki sets polite Edwardian drawing rooms against sudden wildness: a hyena loose at a garden party, a cat that may carry a boy's soul, a pig that settles a garden feud. His beasts are often animals, and his super-beasts are often well-dressed people.

The set opens with The Story-Teller, in which a bachelor wins a train carriage of children with a tale about a horribly good little girl who gets eaten by a wolf. The Open Window, with its invented tale of a hunting tragedy, is also here. Few writers pack so much mischief into so few pages.
beautiful-thoughts:
Elizabeth Cureton arranged this devotional daybook from the writings of Henry Drummond, published in 1892 and inscribed to her friend Helen M. Archibald. Drummond, the Scottish evangelist and scientist, wrote in an epigrammatic style that lends itself to quotation. Cureton's preface hopes a taste of the spring will bring travellers back to the fountain at leisure. Entries run day by day through the year.

January opens on Christianity's wants; a July entry quotes Natural Law in the Spiritual World on man's dependence. Who would stay self-luminous, Drummond asks, knowing the Lord God is a sun? Who would keep a shallow vessel when Christ's well of living water stands open? Many extracts come from The Greatest Thing in the World, his famous meditation on love, though the editorial note admits their pages went unrecorded.
belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne's Belinda, subtitled An April Folly in Three Acts, is a light comedy produced at the New Theatre, London, in April 1918. Belinda Tremayne, her daughter Delia, Harold Baxter, Claude Devenish, John Tremayne and the servant Betty make up its small cast.

The play is set in Belinda's Devonshire country house in late April. The first act plays in the garden, where Betty fastens a hammock for the season, and the later acts move into the hall. Milne, later famous for Winnie-the-Pooh, writes here in the witty, polished manner of the West End stage. Readers who enjoy drawing-room comedy will find Belinda charming and deft.
black-rebellion-five-slave-revolts:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson collected these five accounts of slave revolts from his Travellers and Outlaws, with an appendix of authorities. The Maroons of Jamaica and of Surinam open the volume: the word Maroon was once a word of peril, and terror spread along the skirts of the plantations. Gabriel's defeat, Denmark Vesey, and Nat Turner's insurrection bring the story to American soil.

Vesey's Charleston plot gets the closest narrative. Plans were to be announced only after the evening prayer-meetings on the appointed Sunday. Each leader had his company enlisted and his work marked out. When the clock struck twelve, all were to move: Peter Poyas would seize the arsenal and guard-house opposite St. Michael's Church, and detach men to cut off the city's exits. Higginson, who had commanded a Black regiment, writes slave resistance as military history, with sources, in 1889.
brandes-eminent-authors-of-the-nineteent:
Brandes set aside his grand survey to write vivid portraits of leading nineteenth-century authors, gathered here in English. Many of his subjects were people he had met or known well. Memory and judgment mix in each sketch.

A portrait by Brandes is no dry summary of dates and books. He seeks the ruling passion of a mind and shows it at work. Praise and blame both come sharp and clear from his pen. The book pairs well with Main Currents, giving readers the critic as portrait painter, working from life as much as from the page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptants:
Acceptants were those Jansenists who accepted the 1713 Bull Unigenitus against Jansenist doctrines in Pasquier Quesnel's Reflexions morales sur le Nouveau Testament, without reserve or mental restriction. Jansenius's error had already caused two conflicts in the church. The first, over his book Augustinus, ended with the Pax Clementina of 1669, also called the false peace. The second, beginning with the eighteenth century, was fought around Quesnel's work.

That work first appeared in 1671, a small volume approved by Vialart, Bishop of Chalons, and grew through editions to four compact volumes by 1693. De Noailles sanctioned it in 1695, then condemned it as Archbishop of Paris the next year. The 1699 edition appeared without the changes Bossuet demanded. Meanwhile the doctrine had taken deep root in the French parliaments and in several religious orders, above all the Oratorians, and the entry follows that spread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adventists:
Adventists are a group of six American Protestant sects holding in common a belief in Christ's near return in person. They differ mainly in their understanding of doctrines tied to that belief. Except for Seventh Day Adventists and the branch called the Church of God, they are congregational in government. The sects grew from a religious agitation begun by William Miller in 1831, after minute study of Bible prophecies.

Testing Messianic pronouncements by a strictly historical method, Miller looked for every prophecy's fulfilment in its obvious surface reading. Prophecies unfulfilled at Christ's first coming must be fulfilled at his second, when he would return in clouds to possess Canaan and reign a thousand years on David's throne. Counting Daniel's 2,300 days as years from 457 BC, Miller concluded the world would end and Christ return in 1843. When 1843 passed like any other year, his disciple Snow recalculated, and the movement carried on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-carpets:
Altar carpets ordinarily cover the sanctuary and altar steps of the high altar. Where the floor is marble, tile, or tessellated wood, at least a broad strip lies before the lowest step. Fine rugs are reserved for predella and steps on solemn feasts, and at minimum the high altar's predella, and other altars', should have a rug.

Carpets come off from the Maundy Thursday stripping until Holy Saturday's Mass. During solemn Requiem Masses the sanctuary floor stays bare, though a rug may lie on the predella and before a celebrating bishop's faldstool. Green is mentioned, but any colour may be used. Crosses, saints' images, emblems, and holy monograms must not be woven in, since treading sacred figures underfoot is unbecoming, a rule applying to marble, tile, and mosaic floors too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anabaptists:
A violent and radical body of church and civil reformers, the Anabaptists first appeared at Zwickau in Saxony in 1521. They still exist in milder forms. Their name joins Greek words for again and baptize, yet they denied that the question was rebaptism at all. They held the first baptism, given in infancy, invalid, and so baptized adults who joined them.

They aimed to restore what they took for primitive Christianity. They rejected oaths, capital punishment, and the magistrate's office, and they held Scripture alone as the rule of faith, though private inspiration counted heavily too. Leaders such as Storch and Munzer in Germany, and Denk and Hubmaier in Switzerland, spread the movement through Augsburg, Nuremberg, and Strasburg. Defeat in the Peasants' War of 1525 scattered its first generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustinians-:
The Augustinians of the Assumption, also called Assumptionists, are a congregation born at the College of the Assumption in Nimes. Emmanuel d'Alzon, vicar general of the diocese, founded it in 1843. The group was organized in 1847, took first vows in 1850, and won approval by a brief of November 1864. Its aims were to fight irreligion in Europe and schism abroad. To that end it ran schools, used the press, led pilgrimages, and worked missions in the East.

Its Bonne Presse issued periodicals, pamphlets, and books in numbers, chief among them La Croix, printed in several cities. Its apostolic schools trained students for the priesthood free, and in twenty-five years fifteen such houses gave over five hundred priests to the clergy. French resentment led to suppression in 1900, on a charge of hoarding funds for a royalist rising. Many members left France, while their founder, sent to Constantinople in 1863, always declined the episcopate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bachelor-of-a:
The Bachelor of Arts marks the completion of the traditional college curriculum. In medieval universities the Mastership, or Doctorate, stood as the great academic prize. The Bachelorship seems to have grown from using advanced students to teach younger ones. That teaching counted as preparation for the Mastership itself. Before teaching, the student had to defend a thesis in public disputation. That exercise was called Determination, a rehearsal for Inception to the Mastership.

Two examinations tested fitness first: Responsions, then the sterner Examen Baccalariandorum. The Determination rite also gave the student a special cap and a seat among determiners. Pope Gregory IX's bull Parens Scientiarum of 1231 already calls such student-teachers Bachellarii. The word likely came from the guilds, where French Bachelier meant a young apprentice. The long article follows the degree through Oxford, Cambridge, and later systems, with a full source list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptists:
Baptists are a Protestant denomination found chiefly in English-speaking countries, named for their doctrine and practice of baptism. They hold Scripture the sufficient and exclusive rule of faith and practice, with each believer free to interpret it. No non-Scriptural scheme binds them, and creeds count only as declarations of prevalent views. Their two chief confessions are the Philadelphia Confession of 1688 and the New Hampshire Confession.

The Philadelphia text revises Westminster (1646) in a Baptist sense, appearing in 1677 and adopted at Philadelphia in 1742. It rules in England and the American South, while the North favors New Hampshire's milder Calvinism, adopted in 1833. Church membership, for Baptists, belongs only to those baptized on a personal profession of faith. They reject infant baptism as contrary to Scripture and accept immersion as the sole valid mode.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-adver:
The Book of Advertisements, drawn up by Archbishop Matthew Parker with Grindal, Horne, Cox, and Bullingham, set rules for the queen's church ritual. Parker served from 1559 to 1575, helped by four fellow bishops. It matters for the birth of English Nonconformity and for later disputes over ritual law in the 1800s. On Elizabeth's accession in 1558, Latin services and old Catholic rites still stood, while returned exiles pressed for a worship purged of popery.

The 1559 Act of Uniformity imposed the English Prayer-Book, yet its rubric kept Catholic ornaments from Edward VI's second year. Elizabeth's Injunctions overrode the rubric, and the 1559 visit destroyed vestments wholesale. A bishops' meeting in 1560 kept the cope but dropped the crucifix. When Elizabeth demanded one use in 1565, Parker's Book of Articles, twice delayed, appeared in 1566 as the Advertisements, fixing caps, gowns, and surplices against Puritan protest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-act:
In old Roman law, acts were the registers holding official documents and judges' decisions and sentences. In law, acts mean whatever proves or justifies a thing: records, decrees, reports, and certificates. Canonical acts take their name from church procedure. Acts divide into public and private, civil and ecclesiastical. A public act bears certification by a public notary or office-holder, and may be judicial, part of court procedure, or voluntary.

In contested trials the acts should be judicial, while extra-judicial acts are voluntary, not contentious. Both civil and canon law count as public those acts made before witnesses who acknowledge them before the court. An original sealed document from a community, bishop, or public officer, or a duly authenticated copy, counts as a public act. It binds against anyone, though at times it lays no personal duty on non-participants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-imp:
Impedimentum in Latin means whatever embarrasses or hinders a person, and an army's baggage bore the name impedimenta. In law it means whatever bars an agent's free action or keeps him from performing, or performing rightly, an act the law recognizes. It strikes first at the agent's legal capacity, restraining or even suppressing it, and through that at the act itself, which it leaves defective or even null.

An impediment ends when the agent regains capacity, whether by dispensation or by meeting the act's conditions. It may spring from natural law, divine law, or human law, church or civil. Canon law uses impediment in its strict technical sense only for marriage. Bars to holy orders are called irregularities, though some real bars to orders, like being a woman or unbaptized, are not termed irregular at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charitable-be:
Charitable bequests turn on what courts count as charity. In the Girard will case, Horace Binney called a charitable gift whatever is given for love of God or love of neighbour, free of personal or selfish motive. A fuller legal definition covers gifts applied under existing law for an indefinite number of people. Such gifts may shape minds through education or religion, relieve disease and suffering, or build public works.

Bequeathing itself has its own history. Blackstone's common law gave one third to heirs, one third to the wife, and one third to the testator's disposal, before statutes widened that power. The Statute of Wills and the end of military tenures under Charles II then freed disposition of real property. Restrictions remain: only persons of sound mind may bequeath, with special rules for infants and married women. A bequest that creates a forbidden perpetuity or makes an estate inalienable fails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Joseph Sollier's entry treats the Communion of Saints, from communio sanctorum, fellowship with the saints. It is the ninth article's second clause in the Apostles' Creed: the Holy Catholic Church, the Communion of Saints. Probably the latest addition to the old Roman Symbol, it appears in the Gallican liturgy, in letters now credited to Caesarius of Arles, in Faustus of Riez, and in Nicetas near 400. Critics built rival theories on these traces, some seeing protest against Vigilantius.

Catholic doctrine reads it as solidarity binding the faithful on earth, souls in purgatory, and saints in heaven in one unity. Early inscriptions show its main forms already alive. Later Fathers gave the full dogma. Sollier follows it through the Anglo-Saxon Church, with its devotion to Mary and heavenly protectors. He follows Protestant views too, closing that revival of the old dogma needs the true doctrine of justification restored beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conceptionist:
Michael Bihl's entry follows the Conceptionists, a Clare branch founded by Beatriz de Silva. Isabel of Portugal married John II of Castile and brought kinswoman Beatriz to court. Beautiful Beatriz stirred the queen's jealousy and was imprisoned. Escaping, she fled to Toledo's Dominican sisters, living about forty years there. Devotion to Mary's Immaculate Conception moved her to found an order with twelve companions.

Queen Isabella gave her the castle of Galliana in 1484. The sisters kept the Cistercian rule, adding the Virgin's Office. Beatriz died on 1 September 1490, aged sixty-six. Through Ximenes de Cisneros of Toledo, the order passed under the Franciscans, taking Clare's rule in 1501. Julius II confirmed them in 1506, and Quiñonez framed their constitution in 1516. Houses rose at Torrigo, Madrid, Assisi, Paris. Maria de Agreda, author of The Mystical City of God, wore their white habit, blue cloak, and Marian image.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraterniti:
Florence McGahan's entry covers confraternities of penitents, congregations bound by statutes to fasting, discipline, hair shirts, and like works. They multiplied so far, Rome alone counting over a hundred, that only processional garb color sorts them. The garb runs to a heavy robe with girdle and a pointed hood hiding the face, eye holes letting the wearer see unseen. These groups hold their own statues, churches, and often cemeteries. Aspirants serve probation before admission.

White penitents lead with the Archconfraternity of the Gonfalone, founded at Rome in 1264, when Bonaventure served as Inquisitor-general. Black penitents center on the Misericordia, or Beheading of Saint John. Blue, grey, red, violet, and green groups follow, each with its saints and churches. Mixed-color habits defy grouping. Well represented in France from the thirteenth century, these confraternities perhaps flourished most in the sixteenth, when public penance still shaped devotional life.

Henry Parkinson's entry treats local confraternities of priests, apart from the three great ones given entries elsewhere: the Apostolic Union, the Priests' Eucharistic League, and the Priests' Communion League. A confraternity joins persons for a pious object, linked in brotherhood for religion or charity through prayer, example, and counsel. Purely scientific or literary clergy societies fall outside. English diocesan clergy funds, despite duties to living and dead, fall outside too.

A strict priests' confraternity seeks first its members' personal sanctification. Parkinson then tours the lands. Spain, under hostile government, spurred activity, with the Venerable Congregation of Saint Philip Neri. Portugal holds a Lisbon brotherhood from 1415. Austria holds several groups. France holds secular priests of the Sacred Heart at Issoudun. Rome holds the Pia Unio. America holds many agencies for teeming populations. Spanish America holds its own groups. Germany counts some 1,500 members, with Polish priests in their own Unitas insurance society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desservants:
An entry on the desservants, a class of French parish priests whose meaning changed with the regime. Under the old order the name meant a priest doing parish duty in a vacant parish or for a censured pastor, the stand-in the Council of Trent wanted in every empty parish. After the Concordat of 1801 it named a second class instead, chosen by the bishop without government sanction and removable by him at any time.

Custom, then law, built the system: Organic Articles set up succursal parishes whose holders were not canonically parish priests and drew no state pay. Bishops and prefects fixed their numbers parish by parish, and efforts to win them full parish rights always failed. French discipline on the point stood fixed, and the Separation Law of 1905 left it standing, though some bishops dropped the old terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-discernment-o:
Discernment of spirits is the art of telling which inner promptings lead toward good and which toward evil. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sums up all moral conduct in one rule, shun evil and do good. In the language of ascetic writers, spirits are the pressures that move the will, some from God and some from error, the world, or the self. The entry speaks here of the stricter sense, the spiritual agents that color our acts.

Four sources are weighed, including the human soul itself, whose lower powers war with its higher ones after the Fall. Disturbances of fancy and feeling cloud judgment and must be tested. The brief rules it gathers, admired by masters of the spiritual life, aim to guard the soul against illusion when it seeks to hear God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-distinguished:
Distinguished Jesuits is a roll of honor for the Society of Jesus, naming its saints, blesseds, and famous sons. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with Saint Ignatius Loyola, Saint Francis Xavier, Saint Francis Borgia, and Saint Stanislaus Kostka. It moves through the Japanese martyrs of 1597, the North American martyrs, and Robert Bellarmine, Andrew Bobola, and John de Britto.

Among the blessed stand Peter Faber and the Forty Martyrs of Brazil, priests and students who died together. The entry also notes the order's journals and works, from the Messenger of the Sacred Heart to the Spiritual Exercises. It serves as a quick guide to the men who made the Jesuit name known across four centuries and five continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donatists:
Africa's Donatist schism opened in 311 and thrived for precisely a century, until Carthage hosted its great conference in 411. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces its roots to the persecution under Diocletian, whose first edict in 303 ordered churches destroyed and sacred books burned. A fourth edict in 304 forced all to offer incense to idols on pain of death.

Numidia's governor Florus won infamy for cruelty, and once the storm passed, Christians fell to quarreling over those who had given way. The Donatists held that sacraments from unworthy ministers were void, a claim Augustine answered at length. The entry closes with his teaching that no human fault can void the promises of God to his Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical courts rest on the claim that Christ gave the Church, as a perfect society apart from civil power, the right to legislate, judge, and execute over her members. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry declines to prove that claim here, but draws its consequence with care. If the Church is divinely founded and the Gospels speak true, her rulers may make laws guiding the faithful toward eternal happiness.

As John the Twenty-Second wisely noted, it would be folly to make laws with no one to enforce them. The entry therefore treats the courts that judge church causes, citing Lega, Pierantonnelli, and Keller on practice and history. For students of canon law, it states the ground of a jurisdiction older than most modern states.

Feast days, or holy days, are days kept in memory of the mysteries and events of redemption, of the Virgin Mother, or of apostles, martyrs, and saints. They are marked with special services and rest from work. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses that a feast does more than recall an event or person. It stirs the spiritual life by bringing the event home, so that Christ is born in our hearts at Christmas and we rise with him at Easter.

At set hours Christ summons us to his vineyard. On Good Friday we are nailed to the cross beside him, and at Pentecost the Spirit's gifts come to us. All religions keep feasts, yet none, the entry claims, matches the Catholic Church for a rich and well-built system of festive seasons. It closes with guides from Nilles to Morisot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encyclopedist:
The Encyclopedists were the writers of the eighteenth century who edited or wrote for the Encyclopedie. More narrowly, they were the philosophic party that shared views on philosophy, religion, morals, and society. The work itself was the Dictionnaire raisonne of sciences, arts, and trades. Diderot ordered and published it, with d'Alembert editing mathematics. In its original edition it ran to thirty-five folio volumes: seventeen of text, eleven of plates, five of supplement, and two of index.

It began in 1745 as a French version of Chambers's Cyclopaedia, planned by John Mills and the king's printer Le Breton. Quarrels ended that plan. After an editor resigned, Diderot took charge. He urged a larger, more original work. Diderot, born in 1713, had seen his Pensees philosophiques of 1746 ordered to be burned by Parliament. It questioned Christianity and proclaimed reason independent. His Promenade of a Sceptic, written in 1747, stayed unpublished until after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-recus:
English recusants were people convicted of staying away from the Church of England's services, and this short entry defines the term from statute. The first act to use the phrase Popish Recusants was passed in 1593, restraining such persons to a set place of abode. It defines a recusant as one convicted of not coming to church, chapel, or place of common prayer to hear divine service, against the laws made.

The entry lists the Recusancy Acts from Elizabeth through Charles I, and notes that later statutes counted other offences as recusancy too. In time there were recusants who were not Catholics at all. Some shunned Anglican services for other reasons, a point to keep in mind when reading recusant lists, though most recusants were Catholics. Their numbers were very great: on a single day in February 1690, over seventeen hundred names were presented in Thirsk alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-trum:
The Feast of Trumpets falls on the first day of Tishri, the seventh month. Scripture orders a sabbath memorial marked by the memorial blast of trumpets. Two trumpets appear in the Bible: the silver clarion and the shophar. The shophar, a horn, served the feast in biblical times.

Rabbinic ritual later called the day New Year, Day of Memorial, and Day of Judgment. Through Elul the shophar sounded morning and evening, except Sabbaths. Its call summoned the people to solitude and prayer. Offerings included a bullock, a ram, seven lambs, and a goat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feuillants:
The Feuillants were reformed Cistercians of famously austere, penitential, and prayerful life. Their abbey, founded about 1145 near Toulouse, gave the monks their lasting name. Jean de la Barriere reformed the lax house from 1573. His monks ate barley bread and herbs, slept on planks four hours, and went barefoot.

Barriere's twelve opponents tried poison against him, then left the abbey. Gregory XIII commended the reform in 1581 and confirmed it in 1589. Urban VIII split the congregation into distinct French and Italian branches in 1630. Suppressed in 1791, the Feuillants left many martyrs, confessors, and exiles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-fruits:
First-fruits were the first and best yield of the earth, offered to God before the crop was eaten. The practice was not only Jewish; Greeks and Romans offered first-fruits as well. In Israel the Law named three kinds of offering: Bikkurim, Reshith, and Terumoth. A sheaf of ears was lifted before the Lord at harvest's start, with a holocaust and a libation.

Seven weeks later two loaves from the new harvest were brought to the sanctuary. The choicest fruits — honey, olives, pomegranates, figs, grapes, barley, and wheat — were offered. Custom fixed the gift between one-sixtieth and one-fortieth of the crop. Prepared gifts of oil, wine, dough, and fleece served as a tax for the priests' support.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flagellants:
The Flagellants were bands of lay folk who scourged themselves in public penance processions. The movement first appeared at Perugia in 1260, after plague, tyranny, and prophecies of the end. Men, women, and even children marched stripped to the waist, chanting hymns of Christ's Passion. The penance lasted thirty-three days and a half, in honour of Christ's years on earth.

The pope forbade the processions in 1261, and the first wave died out almost at once. The Black Death of 1347 revived the movement, which spread from Italy across the Alps. North of the Alps it hardened into a heretical sect with its own doctrine and white habit. In Italy the brotherhoods instead settled into charitable confraternities, some lasting to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glosses-gloss:
Glosses, glossaries, and glossarists belong to canon law, where a gloss is an interpretation of isolated words. To gloss is to explain a text word by word, a glossary gathers words with notes upon them, and a glossarist is one who so explains texts. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the school method that turned brief notes into a secondary canonical text.

In canon law, glosses are short elucidations on the important words of the juridical texts in the Corpus Juris Canonici. The Bologna canonists favored the method. Masters' brief notes, first written between the lines, overflowed the margins until they framed the text itself. Later glosses grew into small commentaries, each signed with an abbreviation such as Hug. for Huguccio, and the settled mass became the ordinary gloss, real in authority though not official law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gordon-riots:
The Gordon Riots are the agitation, named for its head and spirit Lord George Gordon, that convulsed London from 2 June to 9 June 1780. The first English Catholic Relief Act of 1778 owed little to feeling for Catholics. A Protestant Association formed to block a Scottish relief bill and repeal the English one. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a petition march that became a week of mob violence.

The Association had already burned chapel-houses at Perth and Edinburgh in February 1779 and won a promise of no Scottish bill. Gordon carried a repeal petition of thirty to forty thousand names to the Commons on 2 June 1780. His procession numbered twenty to forty thousand men wearing blue cockades and carrying blue flags marked NO POPERY. While he demanded an immediate vote inside, his followers pressed upon the House.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermits:
Hermits, also called anchorites or eremites, were men who left ordinary society to live alone in retirement for religious reasons. Some took a disciple as companion, and others settled near inhabited places for food, but the heart of the life was solitude. The pattern predates community monastic life: Elijah stands as its Old Testament forerunner, John the Baptist lived in the desert, and Christ himself withdrew to the mountains.

The eremitic life proper began in the age of persecutions, with St. Paul the Hermit around 250, and St. Anthony made it widely known in the early fourth century. Numbers then swelled across Egypt, Palestine, Sinai, Mesopotamia, Syria, and Asia Minor, and communities grew up among the solitaries without wiping out the solitary ideal. The entry weighs the solitary and community forms of religious life against each other.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herregouts:
Herregouts was the name of three Flemish painters, father, son, and grandson alike, Hendrik chief among them, son of David and father of Jan. David, born at Mechlin in 1603, trained under his cousin Salmier and worked at Ruremonde, where his St. Joseph Awakened by an Angel survives at Mechlin in St. Catherine's church. Hendrik, born in 1633, so loved Rome that he signed some pictures with the added name Romain.

Hendrik joined the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke in 1664, taught many pupils, and painted his best work, The Last Judgment, now at Bruges. His Martyrdom of St. Matthew hangs in Antwerp cathedral, and Brussels holds two more important works. The entry follows three generations of one family through guilds, travels, and churches across the Low Countries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-innocent:
The Holy Innocents are the children named in Matthew's gospel, killed at Bethlehem on Herod's orders after the wise men deluded him. Herod slew all male children in Bethlehem and its borders, aged two and under, matching the time he had learned from the wise men. Matthew links the slaughter to Jeremiah's voice of Rachel weeping for her children.

Tradition swelled the number wildly: the Greek liturgy says fourteen thousand, Syrians say sixty-four thousand, and medieval writers say one hundred and forty-four thousand. Modern writers cut it sharply, since Bethlehem was small, with estimates from about six to twenty. Josephus never mentions the deed, though he records many Herodian atrocities, and the entry weighs why the number stayed so small in sober reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-water-fo:
Holy water fonts are vessels for holy water, of very ancient origin, where archaeology fills gaps left by silent documents. They fall into three kinds: stationary fonts at church entrances, portable fonts for aspersions and sacramental rites, and private fonts kept in homes. The font began as the fountain for ablutions, the cantharus or phiala, set in the centre of the basilica atrium.

Before entering church, the faithful washed hands and feet there, in a rite probably drawn from Judaism and still kept in Muslim lands. When the atrium shrank to a narrow court or porch, the cantharus gave way to a smaller structure. It survives in service mainly at Mount Athos, where the phiala of Laura monastery stands before the entrance. The entry surveys forms, materials, and placement across ages and regions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hottentots:
The Hottentots were one of three peoples of South Africa, alongside Bantus and Bushmen. When the Portuguese first reached South Africa, Bushmen and Hottentots divided what is now Cape Colony, while Bantu tribes lived chiefly north of the Zambesi. Bushmen were physically smaller than Hottentots.

Their origin has sparked much discussion. Some writers suggest a North African origin, and Bleek found points of likeness between Hottentot and North African languages, but the entry calls the evidence too slight to build on. Theal suggests a mixed origin, with intruding males taking Bushman wives. Pure Hottentots, as described by old writers like Kolben, no longer exist, since mixture with other races has changed colour, size, and character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huguenots:
Huguenots is the name often given to French Protestants, though its etymology stays uncertain. Some trace it to the German Eidgenossen, confederates, used at Geneva for champions of liberty and union with the Swiss. That word became eigenots and then huguenots under the influence of Bezanson Hugues, one of their chiefs. Others trace it to Tours, where early Lutherans met near a gate named for Hugon, a count turned in popular fancy into a sinister genius.

From Touraine the name spread through France in hatred and derision for those elsewhere called Lutherans. The entry follows the Huguenots from those naming disputes through growth under Calvin's Geneva, their wars, and their Edict of Nantes settlement. It ends with their later persecutions, giving a full history of French Protestantism from its roots to its diaspora.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-human-acts:
Human acts are acts proper to man as man, as opposed to acts of man, which man performs but not as a rational agent. Thomas Aquinas and the scholastics count only free and deliberate acts of the will as human, a view grounded in psychological analysis. A free act is voluntary: it proceeds from the will grasping the end sought, solicited by the goodness of its object as the understanding presents it.

Free acts also spring from the will's own determination, without inner or outer necessitation. The will can elicit or withhold them even when all requisites of volition are present, determined neither by its object nor by its own habits, but determining itself. Only the will can so determine itself; other faculties lack freedom, though acts they perform under the will's control share its freedom indirectly. The entry builds moral theology on that analysis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-illuminated-m:
Illuminated manuscripts are covered with painted ornaments in several forms. Chapter or paragraph initials may be ornamented very simply or with great profusion of interlacings, foliage, and flowers. They run along the whole page and sometimes depict persons or scenes from everyday life. Margin paintings may carry a scene over several pages.

Borders around the text include interlacing colonnades, the most remarkable example being the Middle Ages' evangelistic canons. Full-page paintings form true pictures, like frescoes or easel pictures, found chiefly in manuscripts very ancient or very recent, from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Rolls of parchment wholly covered with paintings also exist, like the Vatican's Roll of Josue and the Exultet Roll of southern Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-indifferent-a:
Whether a human act can be neither good nor bad is the puzzle at the heart of this moral theology entry. Taken in the abstract, an act judged by its object alone may fit no moral norm and break none, so it can be called indifferent. The harder question is whether that neutrality survives in real life, where a person acts in set circumstances and for a set end.

Bonaventure, Scotus, and the Scotist school answer yes. The entry lines up later moralists who agreed, from Sporer and Elbel to Vasquez, Arriaga, and Archbishop Walsh. Against them stands Thomas Aquinas, whose view the entry weighs in turn. Readers get a clear map of a classic school debate about choice, motive, and circumstance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-pitts:
John Pitts was an English Catholic scholar whose history of English writers remains valuable for its contemporary notices. Born at Alton in Hampshire in 1560, Winchester and New College, Oxford, educated him before he entered the English College at Rome in 1581, and was ordained in 1588. He taught rhetoric and Greek at Reims, taking degrees at Pont-a-Mousson, Treves, and Ingolstadt.

After a Verdun canonry he served twelve years as confessor and almoner to the Duchess of Cleves. He then became dean of Liverdun under his former pupil, the Bishop of Toul. His chief work, Historical Relations on English Affairs, survives in print only in its first part, On Illustrious English Writers, published at Paris in 1619. Sections on kings, bishops, and apostolic men were left in manuscript. Compiled largely from Bale, it must be used with caution except for contemporaries, and he also wrote on laws, beatitude, and pilgrimage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juvenile-cour:
Juvenile courts try children charged with crimes or offences, usually up to seventeen. Below that age they commonly hold exclusive jurisdiction except for capital crimes. Some also commit dependent children or children from unfit homes to custodial care. At Washington and Denver they go further, trying adults who contribute to a child's delinquency and fathers who desert wives and children in need.

The old common law presumed a child under seven incapable of crime, demanded proof of intent between seven and fourteen, and imposed full responsibility at fourteen. Convicted children were then jailed with adult criminals, with deplorable results. The juvenile court replaces punishment with correction, on the ground that a child's character is still unformed and needs forming rather than reforming. Some states run children's trials as separate sessions of ordinary courts, while others, like Colorado, Maryland, and Indiana, have built dedicated tribunals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labadists:
The Labadists were a seventeenth- and eighteenth-century pietist sect, begun by Jean de Labadie (1610-1674). Jesuit-trained at Bordeaux and ordained in 1635, he left the Society in 1639, preached across France, and joined the Reformed Church at Montauban in 1650.

At Middelburg in Holland he refused the Belgian Confession and Reformed authority, founded his own sect, and was expelled. With some fifty-five followers he moved to Herford in 1670 at a princess-abbess's invitation, was banished in 1672, and settled at Altona, where he died. His people, 162 strong, moved to Wiewert in Friesland, peaked near four hundred, planted a failed Surinam colony called Providence in 1680, tried New Bohemia on the Hudson, and dispersed in 1732.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labour-unions:
A labour union's moral standing, this article argues, rests on four tests: its constitution, its end, its results, and its means. A union demanding blind obedience, unlawful secrecy, or support for illicit projects would stand condemned whatever its aims, but no evidence shows today's union immoral in its constitution.

Its two aims are mutual insurance and better terms of work, the second far weightier. Better terms mean wages, hours, sanitation, safety, and kindred conditions, better than workers hold now and better than they would hold without the union. Since those benefits seldom reach, and mostly fall below, what justice owes labour, the chief aim is morally sound. Yet a union already paid its full due wrongs others by using its power to extort more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legends-of-th:
Legend, in its modern loose sense, would cover every untrue tale, but that extension is recent and historically unjust. When the concept arose in the Middle Ages, legend embraced both genuine fact and what modern criticism calls fiction, and German Romantic poets still use it so.

The word grew from Divine Office reading: since martyr days the Church recalled her famous dead in Mass and Office, naming martyrology entries and incidents of lives and martyrdoms. Once the daily reading became a precept, that reading matter was legenda in the precise sense: matter that must be read. After the thirteenth century legenda matched vita and passio, and by the fifteenth the lectionary book fell under legend. Thus legend historically means the story of the saints, though popular embellishment later made it largely fiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legists:
Legists were teachers of civil or Roman law. Besides expounding sources, explaining terms, elucidating texts, and summarizing chapters, they illustrated the many questions and distinctions springing from the Corpus Juris. They drew real or invented cases from the ancient Roman code.

Legal research gained fresh impulse from the twelfth century, legist and decretist were carefully distinguished. Decretist, in the narrower sense, meant the interpreter of church law and commentator on canonical texts, while legist kept the civil and Roman field. The distinction marks the two great medieval law traditions working side by side in schools and courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lights:
Lights, in their liturgical use, have already been treated under Altar-Candles, Candles, Candlesticks, and Lamps. The present article deals only with the general aspect, above all the charge of wholesale pagan ceremonial. How far daytime lights can be traced to the second or third century is not easy to decide.

 Tertullian speaks strongly of the uselessness of burning lamps as piety toward the emperors. About the year 303, Lactantius writes that pagans burn lights for one dwelling in darkness, and asks whether a sane man would offer candlelight to the author and giver of light. St. Gregory of Nazianzus, toward the end of the same century, observes that we should honour God not with blazing light and minstrelsy, but with purity of soul and divine contemplations. It may well be that the writers merely protest against the illuminations of the emperors' cultus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany-of-the:
The Litany of the Saints is the oldest model for all other litanies, a long prayer that calls on Mary, angels, and saints to pray for those who ask. It was already in use in Gregory the Great's sevenfold litany, and Eastern churches used saint litanies as early as the days of Basil and Gregory Thaumaturgus.

Its shape runs from cries for mercy to the Trinity, through Mary and the angels, then apostles, martyrs, and holy men and women of every rank. Next come pleas for rescue from evil and sin, and for grace in every need of life and death. The entry walks through each block in order, so a reader can follow the prayer line by line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuscripts:
Manuscripts are books written by hand on flexible material for a library. Stone and brick books are set aside, as are public acts, which belong to diplomatics. Hand copying ran from remotest antiquity to printing, and Greek copying lasted to the late sixteenth century. Eastern monasteries kept copying well into the nineteenth century, while the latest Western manuscripts date from the late fifteenth.

Materials and form come first: papyrus, parchment from animal skins, and paper said to come from China. Egyptian, Greek, and Latin papyri follow, with their great collections. Making a manuscript meant copyists, free or slave, in monastic scriptoria, from Egyptian houses to Constantinople and the West. Charlemagne's age, the golden monastic centuries of the eleventh and twelfth, and the secularising of copying from the thirteenth are traced. Present homes close it, above all the Vatican Library, founded by Nicholas V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marian-priest:
Marian Priests were English priests ordained in or before Queen Mary's reign, 1553 to 1558, who lived into Elizabeth's reign. After Elizabeth's accession, ordinations in England stopped as surviving bishops were jailed, so without seminary priests the Catholic priesthood would have died out. The harsh statute of 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, which made seminary priests traitors for entering or staying in England, did not touch Marian priests.

They fell under earlier laws, such as 1 Elizabeth, chapter 1. It fined those who upheld a foreign prelate's authority. And 5 Elizabeth, chapter 1, made it treason to uphold Rome or refuse the Oath of Supremacy. Birt's research puts priests holding livings at Elizabeth's accession at 7,500. Most conformed unwillingly, while nearly two thousand were deprived or quit for conscience. Nearly fifty still worked on the mission in 1596. Only James Bell is known to have been martyred.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-queen-of:
Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots, was born at Linlithgow on 8 December 1542 and died at Fotheringay on 8 February 1587. Only legitimate child of James V, she became queen at six days old when he died days after her birth. Tudors tried by war to force a match with Edward VI of England, and Scotland's French alliance shaped her youth.

She married Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, great-grandson of Henry VII with claims to both crowns, but he proved changeable and quarrelsome. After Carberry Hill defeat and Lochleven imprisonment she escaped, only to face fourteen more years of rigorous imprisonment under Shrewsbury and Paulet at Sheffield, Tutbury, and Wingfield. Her fall owed much to over-trust in agent Thomas Morgan's letter-smuggling skill. Babington's plot led to her trial on 14 and 15 October and execution, borne with magnificent courage worthy of her rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massachusetts:
Massachusetts was one of thirteen original United States, formed in 1692 by consolidating Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay colonies. Plymouth settlement began with the Pilgrims' landing on 22 December 1620, and Massachusetts Bay was founded under John Endicott at Salem in 1628. The royal province also held Maine until Congress set Maine off on 3 March 1820.

The state covered about 8,040 square miles with rather more than three million people, of whom 1,373,752 were Catholics. Early exploration included Northmen, Cabots, and Gosnold's 1602 party, while French and Dutch resented English encroachment for a quarter century before the Pilgrims. Colonial population rose from 8,000 whites in 1630 to 70,000 in 1700 and far more by 1750. Education began religious, state normal schools later trained teachers, and Catholic schools grew notably. In 1843 Rhode Island and Connecticut were cut from Boston diocese, and Archbishop Williams's coadjutor William O'Connell succeeded him in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-master-of-art:
Master of Arts is an academic degree higher than Bachelor, tied in origin to the University of Paris, mother-university in arts as Bologna was in law. At first the degree meant only the licence to teach, the Licentia docendi, granted in Paris only by the chancellor of Notre Dame Cathedral or of St Genevieve. Lateran III in 1179 required that licence to be given free to all duly qualified applicants, with fitness judged by the chancellor.

As candidates multiplied and the university grew, presentation before the chancellor became ceremonial, and the degree gained specific academic privileges. At Oxford the degree kept much of its medieval meaning, admitting the holder ipso facto to the Faculty of Arts and the ancient Regency. That Regency was the right to teach, though only in colleges, since university professors were specially appointed. American universities followed Oxford's example in this respect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechitarists:
The Mechitarists, Armenian Benedictines founded by Mechitar in 1712, began as a seeming reform of Eastern monastic life. In 1712, when Rome approved the order, Father Filippo Bonanni recorded two Armenian monks sent by Mechitar to offer Pope Clement XI their humble submission. At that moment no Benedictine rule was named. The monks, of St. Anthony's Egyptian kind, had begun a house at Modon with Mechitar as abbot.

After two years as novices they take the usual vows plus a fourth: obedience to the teacher their superior names to instruct them in Catholic dogma. Many also vow mission work in Armenia, Persia, and Turkey. They live on alms and wear a red cloth cross under the tunic, marked with letters voicing their wish to shed blood for the faith. They elect an abbot for life, wear beards and black habits, and swear to labour in harmony to win schismatics to God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montanists:
Montanists, first called Phrygians or Cataphrygians, were second-century schismatics. Their founder was the prophet Montanus, with two prophetesses, Maximilla and Prisca. Their new prophecy claimed fresh revelations of the Spirit. It imposed strict fasting, forbade flight from persecution and second marriages, and promised a holy city at Pepuza in Phrygia.

Dating the movement turns on an anonymous critic writing soon after January 193. He noted that Maximilla's wars had not come in thirteen years of peace. That places her death near 179 and Montanus earlier still. The entry follows the sect's spread and its condemnation by synods. It covers Tertullian's famous adhesion, its rigorist discipline, and its long survival in Phrygia and the East despite efforts to suppress it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nonconformist:
Nonconformists, in English usage, are Protestants who refuse the rites and government of the established Church of England. Early Puritans balked at the surplice, the cross in baptism, the wedding ring, kneeling at communion, and bishops, some enduring the usages and some resisting at any cost.

After the 1662 Act of Uniformity ejected Puritan ministers from Commonwealth benefices, the name hardened into a label for separatist sects: Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists, and Quakers. The entry traces that split from Marian exiles through the Restoration and beyond. From Elizabeth to the mid-seventeenth century the word marked Puritans, not yet a party name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oil-of-saints:
Oil of saints, also called manna, is oil said to flow from relics or tombs, or oil and water touched to relics and then used for healing. Believers seek cures through the saints' intercession, not through any power in the oil itself, and the custom reaches back to Paulinus of Nola, who died in 431.

Paulinus describes oil poured over martyrs' relics and gathered in vases, sponges, and cloths for the sick, and Paulinus of Périgueux extends the practice to Martin of Tours. The entry catalogues famous oils, from Bari's Saint Nicholas to others, and weighs their evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pandects:
The Pandects, or Digest, form Justinian's chief gift to jurisprudence, and this entry weighs their standing in comparative law. Every logical rule of law, it argues, can be lit from the Pandects, and no other standard of comparative jurisprudence exists. D'Aguesseau's praise is quoted: justice unveiled her mysteries only to Roman jurists, who lend spirit to our usages and reason to our customs.

Tribonian and his fellows compiled the work in a scant three years from thirty-nine eminent jurisconsults, and it abounds in repetition and contradiction. Prost de Royer likens it to a ruined edifice, its pediments gone and columns broken, yet artists still quarry rules and models there. Later pages trace its arrangement, its books, and its sway over modern codes and common law alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-rescrip:
Papal rescripts are written answers from the pope or a Sacred Congregation to queries or petitions from individuals. Some grant favours, others serve justice, as in interpreting a law or naming a judge. A favour may be granted outright in the rescript, or another may be empowered to grant it, or the grant may rest on conditions for an executor to check.

Every petition to Rome holds three parts: the facts, the request, and its reasons. Every response likewise holds three parts: a short statement of the case, the decision or grant, and its reason. Each rescript assumes the petition's claims are true. Deliberate falsehood or hiding of truth voids it, since none should profit by deceit, though mere mistake or ignorance, without malice, leaves the grant standing where good cause exists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parents:
Parents are treated here through their duties to children, from pagan Rome to Christian teaching. In the old pagan world love and reverence gave way to authority and fear. Roman law stretched paternal power to ownership, with rights of life and death, sale into slavery, and seizure of children's goods. Abortion, infanticide, and exposure spread widely, and laws treated them as venial and largely toothless.

Later emperors softened the picture: Alexander Severus curbed a father's death right over adult children, and Diocletian barred selling children. Christianity recast parents as representatives of God, from whom all fatherhood is named, blending love with reverence and grounding children's cheerful obedience. Later pages set out duties of support, schooling in faith, and discipline, and children's duties of respect, aid, and honour toward parents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passionists:
The Passionists, fully the Congregation of Discalced Clerks of the Most Holy Cross and Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, were founded by Saint Paul of the Cross. He was born Paul Francis Danei at Ovada on 3 January 1694. His family moved to Castellazzo in Lombardy when he was ten. There Paul received his call, took the habit of the Passion from his bishop, and wrote the new institute's rules.

Paul wrote the rule as a layman, before gathering companions. He finished it between 2 and 7 December 1720, as if, he said, words were dictated from a professor's chair straight to his heart. In 1725 he visited Rome with his brother, seeking approval. Later pages follow the congregation's growth, its houses, missions, and saints. They stress preaching Christ crucified and keeping His Passion ever in mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patron-saints:
A patron saint is one given by venerable tradition, or picked by vote, as a special intercessor with God. He serves as proper advocate of a place, and clergy and people honour him with special observance. Patron reaches wider than titular: it covers church, district, country, or corporation, while titular marks only a church or institution's patron.
