Max Beerbohm published these tales in London with William Heinemann in 1919. Two tales from the full book, James Pethel and A. V. Laider, stand apart as separate files, so this copy holds the rest. Enoch Soames leads the set.

Soames, a poet of the eighteen-nineties, failed so fully that a full new book on that decade's writing leaves his name out of its index. Beerbohm notes the gap with fond cruelty. His portraits of vain, gifted, and doomed men mix pity with sharp wit, and they rank among the finest short fiction of their age.
side-lights:
James Runciman wrote these essays, issued by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1893 with a memoir by Grant Allen and an opening word by W. T. Stead. John F. Runciman edited the volume. Contents move from letter writers and the decline of literature to the surfeit of books.

Later essays treat people who are down, ill-matched and happy marriages, shrews, and the values of labor. The hopeless poor and waifs and strays close the human side of the set. Runciman writes as a journalist with a warm eye, casting side lights on the manners and strains of Victorian daily life.
sir-thomas-more-or-colloquies-on-the-pro:
Robert Southey published his colloquies with the ghost of Sir Thomas More in 1824, at age fifty, in two volumes with lake views. Cassell's 1887 printing keeps the frame while dropping a few talks whose topics had cooled. Later printings had come in 1829, 1831, and one volume in 1837.

Ghostly dialogues let Southey weigh society's progress and prospects in his later years. One famed talk shows Southey in his library, tracing the course of time through the bodies and souls of books. The editor here keeps all talks on main principles whole, for readers who want Southey's mind entire.
some-chinese-ghosts:
Lafcadio Hearn shapes old tales anew in Some Chinese Ghosts. Roberts Brothers held the 1887 copyright. Hearn gives the book to his friend Henry Edward Krehbiel. Krehbiel was a musician. In Hearn's fond account, he coaxed strange sounds from Chinese strings for him. He also won a song of their own land for Hearn. That song was the song of the jasmine flower.

Hearn's preface begs pardon for the small book. Its stuff, he says, explains its size. He sought weird beauty above all in his choices. He quotes Sir Walter Scott on things beyond sense. Such springs, Scott warned, lose their spring when pressed too hard. Readers who want Chinese letters as a whole must look past this slim set.
songs-for-parents: John Farrar wrote Songs for Parents, and his dedication gives a rhyme each to Barbara, Ted, Wink, and Dick. Dick, he jokes, is not much at reading rhymes and would rather sit and fish, but gets a couple of verses all the same. The contents sort the songs under Songs of Desire, with Summer Explorer, Spring Wish, Ambition, and Dreams, and Songs for Out of Doors, with Parade, Flower Preferences, Parental Advice, and My Garden.
stories-of-achievement-volume-iv-authors:
Volume IV of Stories of Achievement, edited by Asa Don Dickinson, turns to Authors and Journalists. Doubleday, Page and Company copyrighted the set in 1916, and this printing came from Garden City, New York, in 1925, with Robert Burns as frontispiece.

The lives run from Jean Jacques Rousseau and Burns through Charlotte Bronte, Charles Dickens, and Horace Greeley, then on to Louisa M. Alcott, Henry George, William H. Rideing, Jacob A. Riis, and Helen Keller. The contents call Rousseau the man to whom expression was travail. The volume shows young readers how writers and newsmen rose by stubborn work.
strife-a-drama-in-three-acts:
Strife, John Galsworthy's drama in three acts, prints its persons of the play at length before Act I opens in the dining room of the manager's house. John Anthony chairs the Trenartha Tin Plate Works; his son Edgar, fellow directors, the secretary Henry Tench, and manager Francis Underwood stand with the company.

Against them stand Simon Harness, a trades union official, and the workmen's committee led by David Roberts, with a crowd of men on strike behind. The wives, Annie Roberts, Mrs. Rous, and Mrs. Bulgin, are listed too, marking where the strike's hunger lands. The cast list alone frames the play's balance of boardroom, union, and home.
strong-hearts:
George W. Cable's Strong Hearts, dated 1899, holds three tales: The Solitary, The Taxidermist, and The Entomologist. The Solitary first appeared in magazine form under the title Gregory's Island, and Cable opens it with the words of Joseph reading Pharaoh's dream.

Cable speaks through a man of commerce and finance. He says the tales are one tale told several times. Each sets forth one rule in heroic natures and poetic fates. The rule is that religion without poetry is a dead thing. Poetry without religion, he adds, is just as dead. The stories test that rule on lonely, gifted people whose faith and feeling must hold together or fail.
success-with-small-fruits:
E. P. Success with Small Fruits forms Volume Seventeen of Roe's collected works. It is dated 1881 and illustrated. Roe dedicates it to his neighbor Charles Downing. Downing was a fellow horticulturist. Roe says he will count it a privilege to keep learning from him. The book teaches the growing of berries and other small fruits.

Roe's preface gives the book a second aim: to lure men and women back to their original calling, gardening. He jokes that Eve surely helped Adam in the garden and that the first pair ate small fruits at every meal and between. Every generation, he argues, can have its Eden, and many a modern Eve makes a fruitful garden with no help from Adam at all.
such-things-are-a-play-in-five-acts:
Mrs. Inchbald's Such Things Are, a play in five acts, was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, and printed at London in a second edition dated MDCCLXXXVIII, or 1788. A prologue by Thomas Vaughan opens the volume.

Inchbald's advertisement says the subject came from the travels of an Englishman through Europe and parts of Asia to soften the sorrows of prisoners, a work of mercy that stirred wide feeling. She was uncertain where her hero was then at work. So she fixed the scene on the island of Sumatra. An English settlement stood there. Its government let the incidents keep a strict degree of probability. Benevolence, captivity, and cross-cultural encounter drive the comedy.
sword-and-crozier-drama-in-five-acts:
Indridi Einarsson's Sword and Crozier, a drama in five acts, appeared in Poet Lore in 1912 in an authorized translation from the Icelandic by Lee M. Hollander. The play is set in medieval Iceland, where bishops and chieftains fought for rule of the island.

The persons of the play name Botolf, bishop of Holar, and Kolbein Arnorsson the Young, chieftain of the North Quarter, aged thirty-four, with his wife Helga. Around them stand Kolbein Kaldaljos, the bishop's steward at seventy, his son Brand of Reynistad, a woman physician named Salvor, deacons, and henchmen on both sides. Church power and kin power meet head on, and the cast list alone shows how family ties cross the battle lines.
tales-from-the-hindu-dramatists:
R. N. Dutta, a former headmaster of the Metropolitan Institution at Calcutta and author of The Boy's Ramayana, wrote Tales from the Hindu Dramatists, printed at Calcutta by B. Banerjee and Company in 1912. J. S. Zemin, a professor of English literature and former college principal at Calcutta, revised the book.

Dutta dedicates the volume to Sir Justice Ashutosh Mookerjee. The tales retell, in plain English prose, the plots of the classical Sanskrit drama for readers who would not meet Kalidasa and his fellows in the original. Such retellings carried old stories far. They took kings, hermits, and separated lovers from the Sanskrit stage. They set them in the Indian schoolroom. They set them in the general reader's hands. The Lambs' Shakespeare did the same work at home.
tales-of-men-and-ghosts:
Edith Wharton published Tales of Men and Ghosts in London in 1910, with ten stories that mix ghost tales with sharp tales of men and money. The contents run from The Bolted Door and His Father's Son to The Eyes, Afterward, and The Letters.

The Bolted Door opens with Hubert Granice pacing his lamp-lit rooms, tense as he waits for his lawyer at eight. He dreads what the visit will seal, with no way back once the bell rings. Readers get Wharton's cool eye for fear, guilt, and pride, in tales where the ghosts may be real or may live in the mind.
tales-of-the-argonauts:
Bret Harte wrote Tales of the Argonauts, a set of tales from the California gold rush years. Contents include The Rose of Tuolumne, A Passage in the Life of Mr. John Oakhurst, Wan Lee the Pagan, and Baby Sylvester.

The Rose of Tuolumne opens late at night after a dance at Robinson's Hall, as young men ride off in all ways. One girl, loved by many, is left alone in her home at Chemisal Ridge. Readers get Harte's famed gold camp world, with gamblers, miners, and rough kindness, told in tales that helped set how the West was seen in print.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments: A contents list opens Andrew Lang's selection of The Arabian Nights Entertainments, made after the Longmans, Green and Company edition, with dates 1918 and 1898 both shown. Lang's set begins with the merchant and the genius, the fisherman, and the Greek king and the physician Douban. The three calenders and five ladies of Bagdad follow, then the seven voyages of Sindbad the Sailor. The little hunchback, the barber's fifth and sixth brothers, and Prince Camaralzaman with the Princess Badoura close the list.
the-auld-doctor-and-other-poems-and-song:
David Rorie, a doctor, gathered poems and songs written in Scots under a title that names an old doctor. An opening note explains where some pieces first appeared, in journals, student books, and song collections, and notes that one song was issued with music. Titles listed include The Lum Hat Wantin' the Croon and The Pawky Duke.

Early verses joke about a poet who has no time for lofty themes and would rather handle home topics known to doctors. The contents move from the title poem through pieces such as Macfadden and Macfee. Humour, local speech, and medical life shape the collection from its first pages.
the-automobile-girls-at-washington-or-ch:
Laura Dent Crane sent her Automobile Girls to Washington in a 1913 story about checking the plots of foreign spies. Crane is named as author of earlier books in the series set at Newport, in the Berkshires, along the Hudson, at Chicago, and at Palm Beach. A frontispiece shows a scene at the Chinese Embassy.

Chapter titles move from a chance meeting and Cabinet Day to Mr. Tu Fang Wu and a visit to the Chinese Embassy. An arrest, a White House visit, a secret errand, and a girl in danger follow. The girls uncover a confession and a tangled web before matters settle and they return home to Laurel Cottage.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-44-act:
Acts , from the King James Bible, opens by addressing Theophilus and recalling a former treatise about all Jesus began to do and teach. It runs until the day he was taken up, after giving commandments to chosen apostles.

Jesus showed himself alive after his passion by many proofs, seen for forty days, speaking of God's kingdom. Assembled with them, he commands them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promise. John baptized with water, he says, but they will be baptized with the Holy Ghost in a few days. They ask if the kingdom will now be restored.
the-bible-king-james-version-complete-co:
A complete King James Version text opens at Genesis, with the earth without form and void and darkness on the face of the deep. The Spirit of God moves on the face of the waters, in the numbered verse format used through the file.

God says, Let there be light, and there is light, which he sees is good. He divides light from darkness, calling light Day and darkness Night, and evening and morning are the first day. A firmament then divides waters from waters and is called Heaven. Creation in order, day by day, begins a Bible presented book by book in sequence.
the-black-cat-a-play-in-three-acts:
John Todhunter's play in three acts was first acted at the Independent Theatre in London and printed there in 1895. In a preface Todhunter questions why an author should make a speech before the curtain, except that people want views to talk about.

He records a production at the Opera Comique on December 8, 1893, for a special audience, with kind reviews. Critics objected to a tragic ending they thought tacked onto a comedy. Todhunter answers that the end was foreseen from the start and implicit in the subject. A reconciliation between husband and wife, he argues, would have been flat cynicism.
the-blue-bird-a-fairy-play-in-six-acts: Maurice Maeterlinck's fairy play in six acts, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, opens with a long list of characters. Two children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, head the list, followed by Light and the Fairy Berylune. Parents, dead grandparents, and dead brothers and sisters are all named as roles. Household things and animals also speak: Bread, Sugar, Fire, Water, Milk, a dog, and a cat. Trees, farm animals, Time, and Night complete a cast in which almost anything may take a part.
the-bores-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
The Bores is an English form of Molière's verse play Les Fâcheux, dated August 17, 1661. A long first note calls it a character play of a rare kind. Its faults on show are not held by one or two leads. They pass from one figure to the next in quick turns, each gone after a brief show. 

The note then tells how the play was made. Nicolas Fouquet, the finance chief, asked the Palais-Royal troupe for a play to amuse the King, Queen, and court at his house of Vaux-le-Vicomte. Molière had just two weeks to write it. He also had to fit in a dance by Beauchamp, a picture by Lebrun, and stage tricks by Torelli. The note praises how well he met so hard and swift a brief.
the-botanic-garden-part-2-containing-the: The Botanic Garden, Part II, holds The Loves of the Plants, a poem with notes on the thought behind the verse. This is the second form of the book, printed in London by J. Nichols for J. Johnson of St. Paul's Church Yard in 1790. A Latin motto from Claudian stands at the front. In rough sense it says leaves live for love, and palms nod to each other in bonds of love. A front plate shows Flora at play with Cupid.
the-bracelets:
Maria Edgeworth wrote The Bracelets; or, Amiability and Industry Rewarded, put out in 1850 with plates from new designs. Edgeworth had also written Popular Tales and Moral Tales. The tale is set in a fair, quiet part of England. There Mrs. Villars, a lady of clear mind, kind heart, and steady temper, keeps a school.

Twenty young folk live under her care, in full trust from their parents. Her praise is felt as the wage of merit, and her blame as the just fruit of ill acts. Each year she gives a small prize for hard work done well. This year the prize is her own portrait in a small bracelet, dear to all though it lacks gold, pearls, or gems. The two front runners are Cecilia and Leonora, close friends in an uneven way.
the-city-of-domes-a-walk-with-an-archite: John D. Barry wrote this walk with an architect about the courts of a city of domes, but only the Project Gutenberg header is present here. That header carries the standard copyright warnings, donation notes, and the Literary Archive Foundation's details.No pages of the work itself follow the front matter.
the-dark-lady-of-the-sonnets:
Bernard Shaw's The Dark Lady of the Sonnets, dated 1910, opens with a long preface. Its contents range over Thomas Tyler, Frank Harris, Shakespear's social standing, his pessimism, and the idol of the bardolaters. Shaw explains why, in this little piece written for a show aiding a National Theatre as a memorial to Shakespear, he named Mary Fitton as the Dark Lady.

He grants the case collapses on one fact: a portrait of Mary came to light showing a fair lady, not a dark one. Shakespear rubbed in the lady's dark coloring without mercy, he notes. Black hair was as unpopular then as red hair was early in Queen Victoria's reign. Any shade lighter than raven black kills the strongest claim, so Shaw gives up all pretense that his play is history.
the-easiest-way-representative-plays-by-:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way heads a set of representative American plays in this printing. Walter, born in Cleveland in 1874, is quoted with rare candour. He thinks little of the play. He finds no figure in it worth much, save the old agent. He calls it photographic rather than inspired. The first audience at New York's Stuyvesant Theatre, on January 19, 1909, judged otherwise.

Crowds found its portrait of a kept woman's world harsh, true, and purging. The play's force lies in the net that closes round its heroine. It made Walter's name.
the-emancipation-of-massachusetts:
Brooks Adams's The Emancipation of Massachusetts, subtitled The Dream and the Reality, opens with thanks to friends and scholars who fed his research, among them William James. Its contents trace the colony's mind: the Commonwealth, the Antinomians, the Cambridge Platform, the Anabaptists, the Quakers, the witchcraft trials, Brattle Church, Harvard College, and the lawyers.

Adams argues that priestly rule slowly gave way to free thought in Massachusetts. His brother Henry Adams shared the theme. The book, first issued in the 1880s, stays a bold, tart read on Puritan power and its long fade.
the-fatal-boots:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Fatal Boots as a comic tale told month by month, from January's birth of the year to December's winter of discontent. Each month heads a stage in the hero's luck.

The narrator vows that any man's true life would make a good book, then claims far more: strange, sad, unmatched adventures of his own. Yet he grants he never left his home isle nor spoke to a lord who paid his rent. The joke runs through the piece: grand boasts built on small mishaps, with a pair of boots at the root of the hero's woes.
the-folk-lore-of-plants:
T. F. Thiselton-Dyer wrote The Folk-Lore of Plants in 1889 as a brief, ordered survey of the tales and beliefs that cling to plants. His preface calls the field wide and much worked in late years.

Chapters take up plant life, early notions about plants, plant worship, lightning plants, and plants in witchcraft. Demon lore, fairy lore, and love charms follow. Thiselton-Dyer gives a few cases under each head rather than long lists, so the book serves as a handbook. A reader learns why some herbs heal in story, why some trees are feared, and how old rites live on.
the-fugitive-a-play-in-four-acts:
John Galsworthy wrote The Fugitive as a play in four acts, one of his third series of plays. Clare Dedmond, wife of George Dedmond, stands at the heart of the cast.

The cast adds Clare's brother, her friends the Fullartons, her husband's titled parents, a solicitor, a tobacconist, and a writer named Malise. The acts move from the Dedmond flat to Malise's rooms and at last to a supper room at the Gascony. Months pass between the acts. Galsworthy traces a wife who flees a cold, rich marriage and finds that flight has its own hard price.
the-gay-lord-quex-a-comedy-in-four-acts: Arthur W. Pinero wrote The Gay Lord Quex as a comedy in four acts, and only the front matter is present here. That matter lists Pinero's many plays, from The Magistrate and Dandy Dick to The Second Mrs. Tanqueray and Trelawny of the Wells, plus a note that stage rights rest with his agents, Samuel French. No cast list, scene, or speech from the comedy itself can be read in this opening portion.
the-great-adventure-a-play-of-fancy-in-f: Arnold Bennett wrote The Great Adventure. Its subtitle is A Play of Fancy in Four Acts. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of characters, and a list of scenes. The chief figure is Ilam Carve, an illustrious painter. The list names his valet Albert Shawn and his cousin Cyrus Carve, a city auctioneer. It names a priest, a picture dealer, and a millionaire named Texel. It names a widow, Janet Cannot. The scenes move from London to Putney. No dialogue is present.
the-hermits: Charles Kingsley wrote The Hermits. Macmillan and Co. printed the book in London in 1891. It was first printed in parts in 1868. The contents list an introduction first. Lives and studies follow in order. Names include Saint Antony and Saint Paul, the First Hermit. Later names include Hilarion, Arsenius, and Basil. Simeon Stylites and St. Severinus also appear. The list ends with The Celtic Hermits. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
the-history-of-insects: The History of Insects was printed and sold by Samuel Wood at the Juvenile Book-store, No. 357 Pearl-street, New York, in 1813. A line from Genesis about every thing that creepeth upon the earth stands under the title. The pages present give the alphabet in capital, small, and italic forms, then a verse by Barbauld about the insect race keeping a silent sabbath of sleep under a filmy web. Only the title page, alphabet pages, and verse are present here.
the-house-of-rimmon-a-drama-in-four-acts: Henry Van Dyke wrote this drama in four acts, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1908. Only the title page and cast list are present here, so the dialogue does not appear. The cast places the action in ancient Damascus: Benhadad is king, Rezon serves as high priest of the house of Rimmon, and Naaman commands the armies, with his wife Tsarpi beside him. Against them stand figures from Israel, the prophet Elisha and a captive maid named Ruahmah, plus courtiers and the king's fool, Shumakim.
the-hunting-of-the-snark-an-agony-in-eig:
Lewis Carroll subtitled his nonsense poem an agony in eight fits, and he inscribed it to a dear child in memory of golden summer hours. A dedication poem pictures the girl with her spade, then asks her talk to rescue hearts that wiser conversation cannot beguile. The contents name the eight fits: the landing, the Bellman's speech, the Baker's tale, the hunting, the Beaver's lesson, the Barrister's dream, the Banker's fate, and the vanishing.

Carroll's preface begins by playfully defending himself against the wildly possible charge of writing nonsense, treating the accusation as something to answer with mock legal care. Readers meet a crew hunting a creature nobody can define, in verses that parody ballads, courtrooms, and lessons while keeping a child's logic. The poem rewards those who enjoy language tumbling over itself, and its final vanishing lands the joke with a shiver.
the-king-s-arrow-a-tale-of-the-united-em: H. A. Cody published this tale of the United Empire Loyalists in 1922, dedicating it to his own ancestors among them, who came to the St. John River in May 1783. Cody had written The Frontiersman and The Long Patrol. Only the dedication and first contents page are present here. The story itself does not appear. The headings mix war and wooing. When the cannon roared and come and take it open them. Cupid's arrow, the warning, and the twanged bow-string follow. Love's charm closes the list shown.
the-lamp-and-the-bell-a-drama-in-five-ac: Edna St. Vincent Millay wrote this drama in five acts. It marked the fiftieth anniversary of the Vassar College Alumnae Association's founding. She dedicated it to the class of 1917. Only the title page and cast list are present here. The play itself does not appear. It maps a small Italianate court drama. Lorenzo, King of Fiori, and Mario, King of Lagoverde, appear. Guido, Duke of Versilia, is Lorenzo's nephew. A jester named Fidelio, the queen Octavia, and Beatrice called Rose-Red close the list.
the-land-of-footprints:
Stewart Edward White published his African travel book in 1913. He opens not with his own route but with a sharp essay on books of adventure. White divides sporting writers into honest reporters and men who stretch every shot and hardship for effect.

He tells of one hunter who claimed an eland at seven hundred fifty yards. A witness later put the true range near three hundred fifty yards, still a fine shot in any honest telling. White uses the tale to promise plainer reporting about hunting, permits, and travel in little known country.
the-legends-of-king-arthur-and-his-knigh:
Sir James Knowles prepared a popular version of the Arthur legends and dedicated it to Alfred Tennyson in 1862. An addendum by Lady Knowles later explains the book long friendship with the poet. Knowles wrote that Tennyson first Idylls prompted him to seek leave for the dedication.

Tennyson praised the little book, talked Arthur with its author for years, and used it while returning to his own Arthur poem. Knowles retells the Round Table tales in plain prose for general readers. His version helped keep Malory stories in homes that found the old text hard going.
the-life-story-of-insects: Geo. H. Carpenter, professor of zoology in the Royal College of Science at Dublin, wrote his insect life story for the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature in 1913. Only the title pages and a frontispiece caption are present here, showing a gnat transformation in three stages. Larva, pupa case, and adult female appear magnified five times in that picture. The book itself, on insect growth and change for general readers, does not appear here.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Volume fourteen of this Suetonius set contains his Lives of the Poets, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. A contents list names six poets: Terence, Juvenal, Persius, Horace, Lucan, and Pliny. The first life treats Publius Terentius Afer, a native of Carthage who was a slave at Rome in the house of the senator Terentius Lucanus. Struck by the boy's abilities and looks, Lucanus educated him liberally and freed him at maturity.

Suetonius immediately tests a rival story. Some called Terence a war captive, but Fenestella showed that his birth and death fell between the second and third Punic wars, when no such capture was possible. Terence moved familiarly among men of high station, especially Scipio Africanus. The life shows Suetonius correcting legend with dates.
the-loyalists: Jane West wrote The Loyalists, an historical novel in three volumes, printed in London for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown in 1812. West is identified as the author of Letters to a Young Man and A Tale of the Times, under an epigraph urging readers to preserve loyalty and maintain rights. Only the title page and the table of contents for volume one are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. That contents list shows an introductory chapter followed by ten numbered chapters with no titles given.
the-making-of-arguments:
J. H. Gardiner, an assistant professor of English at Harvard, published The Making of Arguments in 1912 and dedicated it to his colleagues on the staff of English A. Chapter one asks what we argue about and why. Argument, Gardiner says, is writing or speaking meant to win other people to your view of a case; that aim is its only essential difference from other writing. Between exposition and argument there is no line.

He proves the point with examples. Huxley's essay on the physical basis of life is one. Arnold's essay arguing Wordsworth the greatest English poet after Shakespeare and Milton is another. Court opinions in the Income Tax and Insular cases complete the set. Argument, he says, works through two tools, conviction and persuasion: first show your view is sounder, then touch the feelings of your readers. The book teaches students to build cases on purpose.
the-mob-a-play-in-four-acts:
John Galsworthy's play The Mob, dated 1914, is present here only as a list of his collected plays plus a title page, so no line of the drama appears. The list sorts his plays into six series. The Silver Box, Joy, and Strife form the first, while Justice stands in the second and Loyalties in the fifth.

The Mob itself closes the third series, after The Fugitive and The Pigeon. Below the list, a title page announces The Mob as a play in four acts, by John Galsworthy, under the heading Galsworthy Plays, Series 3. Act I is named, and the record stops there.
the-movements-and-habits-of-climbing-pla:
Charles Darwin's The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants, in a popular edition published by John Murray in London in 1906, opens with a preface tracing the essay's history. It appeared first, in 1865, in the Journal of the Linnean Society's ninth volume. Darwin reproduces it corrected and clarified, with added facts, and with illustrations drawn by his son George Darwin.

Fritz Muller's observations on climbing plants in southern Brazil receive frequent mention. Darwin also points readers to Hugo de Vries's memoirs on tendril growth, while honestly disagreeing with them. He cannot accept that all tendril movements come from rapid growth on one side. Those caused by touch, at least, work differently, he argues. Bignonia, Cobaea, Echinocystis, and Hanburya are named as beautifully adapted cases worth attention.
the-outcasts: W. A. Fraser wrote The Outcasts, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1901, with illustrations by Arthur Heming. Only the front matter and list of illustrations are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The picture captions reveal animal characters in the northern wilds: Shag, who carried the dog-wolf on his back, A'tim the dog, and Muskwa the bear. A talking wolf promises dinner, so the tale plainly gives its beasts speech.
the-pigeon-a-fantasy-in-three-acts:
John Galsworthy's The Pigeon, billed as a fantasy in three acts, belongs to the third series of his plays. Its central figure is Christopher Wellwyn, an artist, with his daughter Ann. Around them stand Guinevere Megan, a flower-seller, and her husband Rory. Others are Ferrand, a wandering alien, Timson, once a cabman, a canon, a professor, and a justice of the peace.

The acts fall on Christmas Eve, New Year's Day, and the first of April. Act I opens in Wellwyn's studio, a whitewashed room flush with the street. Its skylight is darkened by snow. A fire burns, an easel stands ready, and a Russian samovar hisses beside tea glasses, lemon, sugar, and rum. Through the big window the snowy, lamplit street and the river beyond can be seen.
the-pilgrims-of-hope-and-chants-for-soci:
William Morris's The Pilgrims of Hope and Chants for Socialists was issued by Longmans, Green and Company in 1915. A forward explains where the pieces first appeared. The Pilgrims of Hope ran in The Commonweal between March 1885 and July 1886. Its last instalment still carried the words to be concluded. Morris had given up his plan to revise the whole poem.

The Chants began as a penny pamphlet from the Socialist League in 1885. It gathered songs written for various occasions. One death song honours Alfred Linnell, who died from injuries at a Trafalgar Square demonstration in 1887. Two May Day pieces came from the paper Justice. Several chants had already been reprinted in Morris's Poems by the Way. Together the two works show Morris writing verse meant to be sung and shared by a political movement.
the-piper-a-play-in-four-acts: Josephine Preston Peabody's The Piper, in four acts, was published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1910. Here only the front matter appears, so the acts themselves are absent. The opening pages carry the Hamelin inscription of 1284. It tells how a piper in many-coloured dress led away one hundred and thirty children on June 26. A character list names the Piper and the strolling players Michael-the-Sword-Eater and Cheat-the-Devil. Townsmen include Jacobus the burgomeister, Kurt, Peter the cobbler, and Hans the butcher.
the-playboy-of-the-western-world-a-comed:
J. M. Synge's The Playboy of the Western World, a comedy in three acts, is prefaced by an essay dated January 21, 1907. Synge says nearly every word in it was one he had actually heard spoken, by Irish country folk or in his own childhood nursery. Herds and fishermen fed his ear. So did beggar-women and ballad-singers near Dublin. The wildest sayings in the play, he adds, are tame beside real cabin talk.

The cast lists Christopher Mahon and his father Old Mahon. It names publican Michael James Flaherty, his daughter Pegeen Mike, and the Widow Quin. Action takes place near a village on the wild coast of Mayo. Act I opens in a rough country public-house, where Pegeen sits writing by the turf fire. Synge's preface argues that every speech in a good play should carry the full flavour of a nut or an apple.
the-poor-plutocrats: Mauras Jókai's The Poor Plutocrats, translated from the Hungarian by R. Nisbet Bain, was published at New York by Doubleday, Page and Company under an 1899 copyright. Here only the title pages and contents appear, so the novel itself is absent. Twenty-four chapters are listed, opening with Boredom and A New Mode of Duelling. They move through Bringing Home the Bride and the Cavern of Lucsia. Later entries name the soirées at Arad, the recognition of Fatia Negra, and The Fight for the Gold.
the-pot-boiler-a-comedy-in-four-acts: Upton Sinclair's The Pot Boiler, a comedy in four acts edited by E. Haldeman Julius, is a play inside a play. Here only the cast lists and opening stage direction appear, so the comedy itself is absent. The real-play cast names Will, the author, Peggy, joint author and critic, and son Bill, aged eight. The play-play recasts them as Jack the adventurer, his cousin Bob, sister Jessie, fiancée Gladys, and Belle, a waitress. Several actors are doubled in both layers.
the-power-of-movement-in-plants: Charles Darwin's The Power of Movement in Plants, written with the help of Francis Darwin, appears here by way of its contents pages. The chapters themselves are not shown. Twelve chapters are listed, opening with the circling movements of seedling plants. Later chapters treat how the tip of the root answers touch, how climbing plants move, and the sleep movements of leaves. Movements stirred by light and by gravity close the plan. A detailed contents breaks the first chapter down by plant, from cabbage to oak, pine, and maize.
the-purple-heights: Marie Conway Oemler wrote Slippy McGee and A Woman Named Smith. She published this novel at New York in 1920. She dedicated it to John Norton Oemler. Twenty chapters run from a red admiral and a promise onward. They pass through hard dealings with life and a chapter on Black folk. Cinderella and price-tags follow. Closing chapters are titled for power and for glory. Only the title pages and dedication are present here. A chapter list and a characters heading appear with them. The story itself does not appear.
the-queen-of-hearts: Wilkie Collins frames a set of tales told by three brothers, Griffith, Morgan, and Owen, for a guest they call their queen of hearts. The contents list a dedication letter, an opening dilemma and grand project, then Griffith's tale of a family secret and Morgan's tale of a dream-woman, followed by Griffith's tale of Mad Monkton. Only the title pages and partial contents list are present here, so the tales themselves do not appear. A fuller contents list appears in the companion record of the same work.
the-quest-of-happy-hearts:
Kathleen Hay sends a group of girls toward a great old house called Land's End, set at the edge of a forest, after their father is called away on business. Nora calls the sudden invitation a wild goose chase and notes how little they know of great-aunt Janice Meredith.

Chapter headings promise plans, a tower room with a story of its own, forest exploring, and new friends named Marty and Jerry joining the quest. The opening mood is gloomy, yet the house and its secrets invite curiosity. Young readers get a holiday mystery built around family history and place.
the-ragged-trousered-philanthropists: Robert Tressell maps his novel of working painters in forty-four chapters, from an imperial banquet and a philosophical discussion through financiers, placards, and exterminating machines. Headings name wages, letting rooms, penal servitude, and a great money trick among the episodes. Only the contents list is present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-refugees-a-tale-of-two-continents: A. Conan Doyle divides his tale of two continents into parts. Part one stays in the Old World. It opens with a man from America. A monarch in undress and a held door follow. A house of strife comes next. Later headings set a new world against the old. A rising sun and an eclipse at Versailles appear. Only the title is present here. The opening of the part one contents appears with it. The flight itself does not appear.
the-romancers-a-comedy-in-three-acts: Edmond Rostand's comedy in three acts, Les Romanesques, appears in Barrett H. Clark's translation. Samuel French published it in New York in 1915. Rostand was born at Marseilles in 1868. The play was first performed in Paris in 1894. Cyrano de Bergerac made him widely known three years later. Present here is an introductory note on Rostand's career. A list of persons names Sylvette, Percinet, and Straforel. The dialogue of the play itself does not appear. The note advises late eighteenth-century staging, with Louis XVI costumes.
the-sentimentalists:
George Meredith's The Sentimentalists is billed as an unfinished comedy. Its cast lists Homeware and Professor Spiral first. Arden is in love with Astraea. Swithin and Osier are labeled the sympathetics. Dame Dresden is Homeware's sister, and Astraea is her niece. Lyra is a wife, and Lady Oldlace, Virginia, and Winifred complete the list.

The scene is a Surrey garden in early summer, some sixty years ago. Tall box-wood hedges shade the paths. In scene one the company promenades slowly through the garden. Professor Spiral delivers one of his exquisite orations on woman. A woman who marries takes only one husband, he declares. For her, widowhood does not exist, he argues. Death's punctuation is not the end of her chapter. It is proof of her having a soul, he says.
the-silver-box-a-comedy-in-three-acts: John Galsworthy's The Silver Box, a comedy in three acts, is presented here through its cast and scene list. A sibling record of the same play carries a long biography of Galsworthy instead. John Barthwick, M.P., is a wealthy Liberal, the cast says. Mrs. Jones is their charwoman, and Jones is the stranger within their gates. The time is the present, the list notes. Acts one and two fall on Easter Tuesday. Act three, in a London police court, falls a week later. No dialogue appears.
the-sonnets:
William Shakespeare's sonnets open with a run of poems urging a beautiful young man to marry and have a child, so that his beauty will not die with him. The first sonnet argues that the riper should by time decease while a tender heir bears his memory, and calls the youth his own worst enemy for hoarding his light.

The second sonnet pictures forty winters digging trenches in the young man's brow, leaving his proud looks a tattered weed. The third turns to his mirror and his mother's April prime. Together these opening poems set the sequence's great themes of beauty, time, and succession.
the-spirit-of-the-age-or-contemporary-po: A volume of contemporary portraits, offered here through its contents page alone, with no author's name printed on the pages present. The listed subjects begin with Jeremy Bentham, William Godwin, and Coleridge. They continue through Scott, Byron, Wordsworth, and Malthus. The last names are Southey, Thomas Moore, and Leigh Hunt. The figures named Elia and Geoffrey Crayon close the list. The portrait essays themselves do not appear.
the-spirit-of-youth-and-the-city-streets: Jane Addams wrote this study of young people in modern cities. She worked at Hull House in Chicago. Her earlier book was Democracy and Social Ethics. The study was copyrighted in 1909. This copy is a Macmillan printing of 1930. Only the title pages are present here. They carry her dedication to Louise de Koven Bowen. Bowen understood the needs of city children. She also served as president of Chicago's Juvenile Protective Association. Addams's chapters themselves do not appear.
the-stepmother-a-drama-in-five-acts: Honoré de Balzac's drama in five acts was first staged in Paris on May 25, 1848. Only the list of persons is present here, with the opening stage directions. The Comte de Grandchamp heads the list. He is a Napoleonic general. His second wife Gertrude follows. His daughter Pauline, by his first wife, comes next. The state's attorney Eugene Ramel completes the heads. The scene is the general's chateau near Louviers in Normandy in 1829. A description of the opening drawing-room follows. The dialogue itself does not appear.
the-stolen-bacillus-and-other-incidents: H. G. Wells, author of The Time Machine, gathered these tales for Methuen of London in 1895, dedicating the volume to H. B. Marriott Watson. Only the title page and front matter are present here. Wells's note records where the stories first appeared. Most ran in the Pall Mall Budget. Others ran in the Pall Mall Gazette and St James's Gazette. A contents list names The Stolen Bacillus and The Flowering of the Strange Orchid first. Aepyornis Island and Davidson's Eyes come next. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-jack-and-the-giants: A London edition of 1851, printed by Cundall and Addey, presents Jack's giant-killing adventures with thirty-five drawings by Richard Doyle, engraved by G. and E. Dalziel. Only the title pages and the start of a list of illustrations are present here. The list names scenes such as Jack listening to stories. Giants and fairies fill those stories. The giant Cormoran carries off his booty in another scene. In a third, Jack kills Cormoran by a pit trick. The tale itself does not appear.
the-submarine-boys-trial-trip-making-goo: Victor G. Durham's second book of the Submarine Boys series, dated 1909, sets the boys to make good as young experts. Only the title page, a contents list of twenty chapters, and chapter one's opening exchange are present here: Mr. Farnum, owner of the Dunhaven boat-building yard, says the Pollard was due back at two o'clock, and another voice notes it is within five minutes of that hour. The titles promise a missing submarine and a race for mixed prizes, so the trial trip itself does not appear.
the-thirteenth-chair-a-play-in-three-act: Bayard Veiller's Thirteenth Chair, a play in three acts, appears here in Samuel French's London acting edition of 1922. The pages present are the licensing terms, not the play: amateur companies must apply to French for a licence, at five guineas, with later performances reduced to three. A note adds that costumes and wigs can be hired from Charles H. Fox in Long Acre. A production line records the play's first staging at the Duke of York's Theatre on October the sixteenth, then breaks off. Veiller's dialogue itself is absent.
the-title-a-comedy-in-three-acts: Arnold Bennett's Title, a comedy in three acts, was published by Chatto and Windus in 1918. This record holds its opening leaves. They give a cast list, the act settings, and the first stage direction. The cast names Mr. and Mrs. Culver, their children Hildegarde and John, plus Tranto, Miss Starkey, and Sampson Straight. All three acts play in the Culvers' West End sitting-room across three days around New Year. Act one begins with Hildegarde writing at a desk, and there the pages stop, before Bennett's dialogue can start.
the-united-states-bill-of-rights-the-ten:
Congress passed the ten original amendments to the United States Constitution on September 25, 1789, and ratification followed on December 15, 1791. The opening amendment bars laws establishing religion or blocking its free exercise. It also protects speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitions for redress of grievances.

Later amendments shown guard the right to keep and bear arms and forbid soldiers quartered in homes during peacetime without consent. Another secures people against unreasonable searches and requires warrants on probable cause. The fifth demands grand jury indictment for serious crimes, bans double jeopardy and forced self-witness, and promises due process. A sixth begins the rights of the accused in criminal prosecutions.
the-valley-of-the-giants:
Peter B. Kyne tells a California redwood story in The Valley of the Giants, illustrated by Dean Cornwell and dedicated to his wife. Chapter one lands in the summer of 1850, when a topsail schooner leaves a lone man on the beach under Trinidad Head. John Cardigan carries a squirrel-rifle, an axe, and a canvas pack into the timber.

Kyne announces the whole arc at once: Cardigan will pioneer, love, lose his wife, win success, and face ruin late in life. Then his son Bryce takes up the fight to save the family heritage, leading a forlorn hope for an ideal rather than wealth. The redwood belt itself, four hundred miles of giant trees, supplies the scale.
the-well-of-the-saints-a-comedy-in-three:
J. M. Synge sets his comedy The Well of the Saints in a lonely mountain district of eastern Ireland, a century or more ago. The play was first staged by the Irish National Theatre Society under W. G. Fay, and production notes date that staging to February 1905 at the Abbey Theatre. Fay himself played Martin Doul, with Emma Vernon as Mary Doul and Sara Allgood as Molly Byrne.

The persons list introduces Martin and Mary Doul as weather-beaten blind beggars, husband and wife. Timmy the smith, two handsome girls, Mat Simon, and a wandering friar called the Saint complete the cast. Act one opens on a roadside with big stones and a ruined church doorway, where the Douls grope in and sit down together.
the-world-english-bible-web-acts:
Acts, book forty-four of the World English Bible, addresses a reader named Theophilus. The writer recalls his first book about Jesus. That account covered all Jesus did and taught. It ran until the day he was taken up. Before that, Jesus showed himself alive for forty days. He spoke about God's Kingdom during those appearances.

Jesus orders the apostles to stay in Jerusalem. They must wait for the Father's promise. John baptized with water, he explains, but they will receive the Holy Spirit. The apostles ask about restoring Israel's kingdom. Jesus redirects them toward witness and power. The early church's story unfolds from that waiting room.
three-young-knights:
Annie Hamilton Donnell opens her story at the Eddy farm, where the last wisp of hay is finally in the mows. Jot and Kent cheer, while Old Tilly surveys the finest hay in Hexham County with honest pride. Father Eddy joins the shouting for liberty after haying.

He announces a fortnight's holiday, hires Esau Whalley for chores, and pays each boy five dollars. The three round, brown faces shine at the unexpected notes. Readers get a wholesome boys' adventure beginning with farm work finished, wages paid, and three young knights suddenly free to celebrate as they choose.
through-the-fray-a-tale-of-the-luddite-r:
G. A. Henty set his tale of the Luddite riots in Marsden, Yorkshire, opening at Mr. Hathorn's academy in 1807. Boys stream out at one o'clock in tight-kneed breeches and close jackets, many with tear-stained, dirt-grimed cheeks. The cane was then the one known method of teaching.

Hathorn's cane whizzes and finds tender places unerringly, and passers-by hear cracks, silence, or shrieks. His boys hate him yet know flogging prevailed everywhere. Readers get a boys' historical novel where school cruelty frames the industrial unrest named in Henty's title, the Luddite riots.
touch-and-go-a-play-in-three-acts:
D. H. Lawrence prefaced his three-act play with an essay on a people's theatre, which he insists does not yet exist. The name is chosen, he jokes, but the baby is not even begotten. He builds a syllogism: cheap seats, good plays, therefore a people's theatre.

Lawrence argues cheap seats need not mean proletarian swank or profiteering, since nobody truly consents to high prices without hoping to recover them. He also mocks the word good, asking whose goodness judges a play. Readers get Lawrence's combative theatre theory before the drama, aimed at capital, labour, and squeezed decent people alike.
trevelyan-england-under-stuarts:
G. M. Trevelyan first published England under the Stuarts in 1904. Readers here meet the 1926 reprint of that lasting classic work. Seventeenth-century England, from James I to William III, fills its span.

Civil war, the republic, Restoration, and the Glorious Revolution pass in review. Trevelyan writes with grace, pace, and a liberal love of freedom. His kings and crowds live on the page in bright, quick strokes. Generations learned the Stuart age from this single, fluent volume. Its charm and clarity made dry politics read like a national novel. Trevelyan's balance of story and fact set a standard for popular history.
tristan-and-isolda-opera-in-three-acts:
Richard Wagner's Tristan and Isolda appears in the Oliver Ditson grand opera libretto series, with German and English text and the music of the leading motives. The transcriber notes that the German text is not included in this ebook file. Boston, New York, and Chicago imprints of the Ditson houses share the title pages.

After the title pages comes a prose story of the opera in sequence. Its first act begins the tale of the lovers aboard ship. Singers and students used such librettos to follow the words and themes in the theatre. The three-act structure of Wagner's music drama is laid out plainly for English readers before the verse begins.
true-stories-about-dogs-and-cats:
Mrs. Follen returns to the Chilton family for True Stories About Dogs and Cats, illustrated by Billings. Mary Chilton, a widow in a quiet New England village, raises her sons Frank, nine, and Harry, seven. The narrator pauses to give their names and ages so young readers know the boys were real.

The mother holds a talk with her boys each night about the day that has passed. Sometimes she tells stories, and sometimes they repeat poetry. Her rule for conduct is short: stop and think. Frank checks himself when Harry warns that mother will be sorry. The animal tales grow out of these evening talks in the same household as her Travellers' Stories.
two-poets:
Honore de Balzac's Two Poets, translated by Ellen Marriage, forms part one of the Lost Illusions trilogy. A preparer's note maps the whole: Lucien, his sister Eve, and his friend David in provincial Angouleme. Part two takes Lucien to Paris, and part three returns to Eve and David, with a further book continuing Lucien's story.

Balzac dedicates the volume to Victor Hugo, praising his victorious name as a shield against jealous journalism. The novel opens in an Angouleme printing office before the Stanhope press and ink roller reached small provincial shops. The primitive wooden press still rules there. Printing, paper mills, and ambition meet in the first pages of Lucien's rise.
un-doc-initiative-on-the-safe-transporta:
The Initiative on the Safe Transportation of Grain and Foodstuffs from Ukrainian Ports was signed at Istanbul on 22 July 2022. War had shut Ukraine's Black Sea ports since February. Grain sat in silos while world food prices spiked. Türkiye, Russia, and Ukraine signed the deal, which the UN chief had proposed.

The deal opens three ports: Odesa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhny. A joint centre in Istanbul, run with the United Nations, watches each ship's path. Mixed teams in Türkiye search ships both ways for arms or stowaways. Ships move along a marked sea lane, safe from attack. The pact runs 120 days at a time and renews on its own unless a party pulls out.
uncle-vanya-scenes-from-country-life-in-:
Anton Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, scenes from country life in four acts, opens with its cast. Alexander Serebrakoff, a retired professor, heads the list, with his young wife Helena and his daughter Sonia. Vanya himself is the professor's brother-in-law, son of the widowed Mme. Voitskaya. Dr. Astroff and the impoverished landowner Telegin complete the household's circle.

Act one sets a terrace table for tea on a cloudy afternoon, samovar and guitar at hand. Marina, the old nurse, knits a stocking and pours tea for the pacing Astroff. The scene is Serebrakoff's country place. No translator is named on the pages shown, and the play's weary opening conversation begins at the tea table.
under-the-skylights:
Henry Blake Fuller wrote the three long stories gathered in Under the Skylights. A prefatory note explains that the closing piece, about Dr. Gowdy and a squash, first ran in Harper's Magazine, while the rest appears in print for the first time. The lead story follows Abner Joyce, a young novelist whose first book, This Weary World, wins him a place in letters at once.

Fuller's opening pages describe Joyce as grim, rugged, and sincere, a man who cared less about style than about setting the world's wrongs right. He believed people were fine one by one and wrong only in crowds. The middle story pits Little O'Grady against the Grindstone. Together the pieces give a picture of ambition, work, and city life, drawn with dry humor and close attention to character.
us-constitution-bill-of-rights:
The Constitution of the United States was written at Philadelphia in 1787 and took effect in 1789. The text here adds the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791. The wording follows the edition kept by the United States House of Representatives.

The main text builds the federal government: Congress, the presidency, the courts, and the rules binding them together. It also sets how states relate to the union and how the text itself can be amended. The Bill of Rights guards speech, worship, arms, fair trials, and more against federal power. It remains the supreme law of the country.
vanity-all-is-vanity-a-lecture-on-tobacc: Elder J. J. Cranmer, editor and owner of the Gospel Monitor at Hannibal, Missouri, offered the public a lecture called Vanity, All Is Vanity. Its subject is tobacco and its effects. Pages present here are poster-like front pages only, so the lecture itself is not shown. They carry slogans in bold type. One says habit is harder to serve than a king, taxing body, mind, and pocket daily. A poem on the pages calls tobacco users slaves the leaf has bound, from king to farmer.
vautrin-a-drama-in-five-acts:
Honore de Balzac wrote Vautrin, a drama in five acts. The Porte-Saint-Martin Theatre in Paris first played it on March 14, 1840. His preface, penned five days after the first night, admits how hard it is to write one. Every reader, he says, has already written his own preface to the play. The author's single voice must fall short of so many views. A cannon shot, he adds, falls short of fireworks in the same way.

Balzac asks who can gloss the work. His answer: its only true commentator is the actor Frederick Lemaitre, who played the lead. He touches, too, on the official ban that had delayed the staging. Petty tyranny, he calls it, the besetting sin of governments that rule under a constitution. The preface shows a playwright both proud and sore. He defends a play about his great rogue Vautrin before the critics have cooled.
verses-and-sonnets: Hilaire Belloc published Verses and Sonnets at London with Ward and Downey in 1896, and dedicated the book to John Swinnerton Phillimore. The header line of the file gives the same year, 1896. Pages present here give the title page and the first entry of the contents, a poem called The Night at page eleven, so the verses themselves are not shown. Belloc was twenty-six that year, and the slim volume stands near the start of a long career in verse, essays, and history.
wandering-ghosts:
F. Marion Crawford's full set of weird tales came out in 1911, the year of his death in print form here. He had writ the tales through his long life as a star of the romance world. The set holds the whole of his work in the ghost and horror kind.

'The Upper Berth' traps a man in a ship's bunk with a wet, cold thing that shares it. 'For the Blood Is the Life' is a vampire tale of Italy, and 'The Screaming Skull' a tale of a skull that will not rest. The set is the one book to own for Crawford's ghost craft.
waste-a-tragedy-in-four-acts:
Granville Barker wrote Waste, a tragedy in four acts. Sidgwick and Jackson issued it at London in 1909, and the play is dated within to 1906 and 1907. The action opens at Shapters, George Farrant's house in Hertfordshire. It is ten o'clock on a Sunday evening in summer. Mrs. Farrant sits at her piano by the window, behind a little screen. She is a woman of serene face and puzzled brow, an almost ideal hostess in her own home.

Her eyes pass over Lucy Davenport, a girl of twenty-three in a low chair by the table. Lucy is undefeated in anything as yet, and so unsoftened. A closed book rests on her lap. Mrs. O'Connell lounges on one sofa, and Miss Trebell sits opposite. Barker builds his drawing room person by person, before the talk turns to the politician at the play's dark heart.
wee-macgreegor-enlists:
J. J. Bell wrote Wee Macgreegor Enlists in 1916, a comic tale of a Glasgow lad gone to soldier in the great war. He dedicated it to his wife. His contents trace the lad's path: arms and the maid, breaking it gently, first blood, and the ring. In uniform, correspondence, and conscience and a cocoa-nut follow. Fondest love from Maggie, a serious reverse, and the real thing at last come late. No hero, yet happy, ends the list.

Chapter one, Arms and the Maid, brings the hero through a gateway flanked by tall recruiting posters. He comes rather hurriedly. He is a youth of no great stature but sturdy build, with bright brown eyes and a fresh complexion. He is sweating a little, though the dull morning is cold. Bell writes Glasgow speech and Glasgow hearts, and turns enlistment into both joke and pride.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Acts is book 44 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The writer speaks to Theophilus and links back to his first book on Jesus. That book told what Jesus did and taught up to his rising into heaven. Here the tale picks up with the apostles in Jerusalem.

Jesus tells them to wait for the Father's promised gift. They will be baptized with the Holy Spirit in a few days. Power will make them witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Two men in white then tell the watching group that Jesus will return. Weymouth's plain style suits the fast story well.
witchcraft-and-devil-lore-in-the-channel: Only the title page is present here for John Linwood Pitts's Witchcraft and Devil Lore in the Channel Islands, so the court records themselves do not appear. Pitts drew the book from the official records of the Guernsey Royal Court. He adds an English translation and a historical introduction. Guernsey printers issued it in 1886. A verse from Exodus heads the title page: thou shalt not suffer a witch to live. Pitts also edited patois poems of the islands and dialect versions of scripture.
wolfville-nights: Alfred Henry Lewis published this third Wolfville gathering in 1902. Pages present here give a contents list and a dedication to William Greene Sterett, but no tale text. Chapter titles promise Faro Nell dealing bank, a ghost at the Bar-B-8 ranch, and Colonel Sterett's panther hunt. Other titles name Dave Tutt, Tucson Jennie, and Dan Boggs. The cow town cast returns, judging by the titles, yet the stories themselves stay absent here.
write-it-right-a-little-blacklist-of-lit:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this 1909 manual on precise English. His stated aim is to teach writers to pick the exact word. Good writing, he says, is clear thinking made visible. A reader should not merely be able to grasp the sense. The words should force the right sense. Bierce distrusts bloated dictionaries and loose popular usage alike.

The volume works mostly by example rather than rule. Quoted phrases mark usage Bierce rejects. He allows some slang and informal speech in light writing, used with restraint. Serious writing gets stricter limits. Readers get sharp, funny guidance on faults to cut.
